questions.title: Choosing Between #Temp Tables, Table Variables, and CTEs Inside a Stored Procedure
questions.prompt: You're writing a complex reporting stored procedure. Partway through, you compute an intermediate result set of roughly 200,000 rows that gets referenced three separate times later in the procedure, filtered differently each time, and would benefit from its own index on one of its columns. A junior developer on your team used a CTE for it because 'that's what we always use.' Explain why that choice is likely to hurt performance here, what you'd use instead and why, and the one scenario where a table variable would actually be the better choice over a temp table.
questions.modelAnswer:
A CTE isn't a stored, materialized result at all -- it's inlined into the statement that references it, and if you reference the same CTE three separate times, SQL Server may well re-run its underlying query three separate times (unless it happens to decide to spool the result on its own, which isn't something you can rely on or control). For a 200,000-row intermediate result referenced three times with different downstream filters, that risks recomputing the same expensive logic three times over, and a CTE also can't carry its own index -- so if the column you'd filter or join on isn't already well-served by indexes on the base tables, every one of those three references pays that cost independently.

A #temp table is the right choice here. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, which means two things that matter directly to this scenario: SQL Server maintains real statistics on it, so the optimizer can build a genuinely informed plan for each of the three later queries against it (rather than guessing), and you can explicitly CREATE INDEX on it -- so the column those three downstream queries filter or join on can actually be indexed, turning three potential scans into three seeks. At 200,000 rows, this is squarely the 'thousands of rows, reused more than once, might need its own index' case.

A table variable would be the better choice only when the intermediate set is small -- a handful to a few hundred rows -- and you're specifically trying to avoid statement recompilation inside a stored procedure. Historically, SQL Server assumed a table variable held exactly one row for costing purposes (pre-2019 compatibility levels, or without the newer deferred-compilation improvements), which is actually fine when the set really is tiny, but would badly under-allocate resources at 200,000 rows -- the opposite of what you want here. Table variables also aren't rolled back by an enclosing ROLLBACK, which occasionally matters for specific logging/auditing patterns, but that's a narrower reason to choose one and isn't the deciding factor in this scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the junior developer: the CTE choice makes sense as a habit, but it's working against them here specifically because of how many rows there are and how many times it gets used. A CTE doesn't actually store anything -- every time you reference it, SQL Server might just re-run the query behind it from scratch, and it has no index of its own. If we're touching this 200,000-row set three separate times with three different filters, we could be paying for that underlying computation three times, and none of those three references get to use an index on it even if one would help a lot.

My recommendation is a #temp table instead: dump that intermediate result into it once, put an index on whatever column the three downstream queries actually filter or join on, and now each of those three references gets a real seek against real statistics instead of SQL Server guessing. That's exactly the profile -- meaningful row count, reused multiple times, benefits from its own index -- where a temp table wins clearly.

I'd also tell them table variables aren't wrong, just wrong for this case -- they're great when the set is genuinely small and you're inside a procedure trying to avoid a recompile every time row counts shift. The catch is that SQL Server has historically assumed a table variable holds about one row when it's building a plan, which is totally fine for a small set but would be a disaster at 200,000 rows -- the optimizer would badly under-allocate for a set that size, and the plan quality would suffer for every one of those three references, not help it.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a CTE out of habit regardless of row count or reuse pattern
Not realizing a CTE referenced multiple times may re-run its underlying query each time
Assuming a table variable always outperforms a temp table because it 'sounds lighter weight'
Putting a large, reused intermediate set into a table variable and getting a poor plan from the one-row cardinality assumption
Forgetting that only a #temp table supports an explicit CREATE INDEX statement after the fact
keyPoints: CTEs are inlined and re-evaluated per reference, not materialized or indexed
#Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and support explicit indexes
200,000 rows reused three times with filtering is a textbook #temp table case
Table variables historically get a one-row cardinality assumption, poor for large sets
Table variables fit small sets inside procedures where avoiding recompilation matters most

Recommends a #temp table and justifies it with statistics/indexing
Explains the risk of recomputation across three CTE references
Correctly identifies the scenario where a table variable wins
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Explaining Context Transition in a Calculated Column
questions.prompt: A colleague doesn't understand how this calculated column can possibly work, since a calculated column is supposed to only see row context: Customer Segment = IF(CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey])) < 2500, "Low", "High"). Explain, step by step, what actually happens for one customer row.
questions.code:
Customer Segment =
IF (
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] ),
        ALLEXCEPT ( Customer, Customer[CustomerKey] )
    ) < 2500,
    "Low",
    "High"
)
questions.modelAnswer: Context transition is exactly the bridge that makes this work. For one specific customer row: the formula starts in row context, since DAX is evaluating this expression for one particular CustomerKey. The moment CALCULATE is invoked, it triggers context transition - the current row context, this one customer, is converted into an equivalent filter context, as if a filter had been applied limiting the whole model to that one CustomerKey. ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey]) then clears every other filter that might be active on the Customer table while deliberately preserving the context-transition filter just created on CustomerKey - this matters because it's what protects the expression from unrelated filters if this logic were ever reused in a visual, even though a calculated column itself has no report-level filters to begin with. SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) now aggregates across whatever rows of Sales are reachable through the Customer-Sales relationship under that one-customer filter - that is, all of that customer's sales, nothing else. IF compares the result to 2500 and labels that row. This repeats independently for every row in Customer - row context in, filter context out, one customer at a time - which is exactly why a calculated column, which is 'supposed to' only see row context, can still produce a result that depends on aggregating an entirely different table: CALCULATE is what converts between the two context types, and it's invisible/automatic for a bare measure reference but explicit here because CALCULATE is written directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk them through it one customer at a time. We start in row context - DAX is sitting on one specific CustomerKey. As soon as it hits CALCULATE, that row context gets converted into a filter context scoped to just that one CustomerKey - that conversion is context transition, and it's the whole reason this works. ALLEXCEPT then strips away any other filters on the Customer table but specifically keeps the one context transition just created, so the filter context going into SUM is exactly 'this one customer.' SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) then totals every sale tied to that customer through the relationship, and IF labels the row based on that total. Every row repeats this independently. So the calculated column isn't magically seeing filter context on its own - CALCULATE is explicitly converting its row context into one, which is the same thing that happens invisibly whenever you reference a plain measure from inside a calculated column.
questions.example: Simpler illustration of the same mechanism without ALLEXCEPT: a calculated column Row Total = [Some Measure] works for the same reason - referencing a measure from row context implicitly wraps it in CALCULATE, triggering context transition automatically, with no CALCULATE visible in the formula at all.
commonMistakes: Saying calculated columns 'can't see filter context' without explaining that CALCULATE is what bridges the two
Missing that a bare measure reference in row context triggers the same mechanism implicitly, without a visible CALCULATE
Thinking ALLEXCEPT is what causes context transition, rather than CALCULATE itself
Describing the behavior without walking through it per-row
keyPoints: Context transition converts row context into an equivalent one-row filter context
It is triggered specifically by CALCULATE evaluating inside row context
A bare measure reference inside row context triggers it implicitly via an invisible wrapping CALCULATE
ALLEXCEPT here preserves the context-transition filter while clearing other filters on the table
The whole calculation repeats independently for every row

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the trigger for context transition (CALCULATE in row context)
Walks through the five-step mechanism accurately
Explains the implicit-CALCULATE case for bare measure references
Clear, row-by-row framing

questions.title: AVERAGEX vs. a Plain AVERAGE Measure
questions.prompt: A report needs the average order value, where order value is the sum of all line items on an order, not a single stored column. Explain why CALCULATE(AVERAGE(Sales[LineTotal])) gives a different (and wrong) answer than an AVERAGEX-based approach, and write the correct measure.
questions.code:
Average Order Value =
AVERAGEX(
    VALUES(Sales[OrderID]),
    CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[LineTotal]))
)
questions.modelAnswer: CALCULATE(AVERAGE(Sales[LineTotal])) averages across line items, not orders - every individual line of every order counts as one data point, so an order with ten small line items pulls the average down and an order with one huge line item pulls it a different way, regardless of what each order actually totaled. That's the wrong grain entirely: the business question is 'average order value,' and the unit of analysis has to be the order, not the line. The fix is to iterate at the order grain: use VALUES to get one row per order, compute each order's total with CALCULATE(SUM(...)) inside that per-order context, and then AVERAGEX that result across orders - AVERAGEX evaluates its expression once per order, the correct grain, and averages those per-order totals rather than the raw line-level column. This is the same 'does the value already exist as one column, or does it need computing per group first' question that distinguishes SUM from SUMX, just applied to AVERAGE: because order value genuinely doesn't exist as a single column anywhere, a plain AVERAGE, even wrapped in CALCULATE, is aggregating the wrong thing from the start - no filter context modifier fixes that, because the problem isn't the filter, it's the grain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem isn't a filter-context issue at all, it's a grain mismatch. AVERAGE(Sales[LineTotal]) is averaging over line items, so an order with a lot of small lines and an order with one big line pull the average in different directions that have nothing to do with what either order actually totaled - CALCULATE wrapped around it doesn't change that, because CALCULATE only changes filters, not what's being averaged. What actually fixes it is averaging at the order grain: I'd use VALUES(Sales[OrderID]) to get one row per order, compute each order's total inside that context with CALCULATE(SUM(...)), and let AVERAGEX average those per-order totals instead of the raw line rows. That's the same idea as SUMX versus SUM, just one level up - the value I need doesn't exist as a column, it exists as a calculation at a specific grain, so I need an iterator that operates at that grain.
questions.example: If Order 1001 has three lines totaling $300 and Order 1002 has one line totaling $900, the wrong measure averages across 4 individual line amounts; the correct measure averages {$300, $900} = $600 - a materially different answer.
commonMistakes: Averaging at the line-item grain when the business question is about orders
Assuming wrapping AVERAGE in CALCULATE fixes a grain problem - it only changes filter context, not the unit being averaged
Forgetting that CALCULATE(SUM(...)) inside AVERAGEX's expression triggers context transition for each OrderID, which is exactly what makes the per-order total correct
Using SUMX instead of AVERAGEX when the goal is specifically an average across the grouped values, not a sum
keyPoints: Plain AVERAGE averages at whatever grain the underlying column exists at - here, line items, not orders
AVERAGEX lets you choose the correct grain by supplying the table to iterate (one row per order)
Context transition inside AVERAGEX's expression (via CALCULATE/SUM) computes each order's total correctly before averaging
No filter modifier fixes a wrong-grain measure - the fix is changing what's being iterated

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the grain mismatch as the root cause
Correct AVERAGEX-based measure at order grain
Explains why CALCULATE alone doesn't fix a grain problem
Concrete numeric example showing the discrepancy

questions.title: Choosing Between ALL, ALLEXCEPT, and ALLSELECTED
questions.prompt: A report has a table visual broken out by Product Category and Year, on a page already filtered to Europe via a report-level filter. Write three measures that each answer a different question: (1) each cell's share of the true dataset-wide grand total, (2) each cell's share of the total for everything currently visible given the Europe filter, ignoring only the visual's own category/year breakdown, and (3) a measure that behaves like #1 but written using ALLEXCEPT instead of ALL. Explain the difference between all three.
questions.code:
%% of Grand Total (ALL) = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales)))

%% of Visible Total (ALLSELECTED) = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLSELECTED()))

%% of Grand Total (ALLEXCEPT) = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(Sales)))
questions.modelAnswer: These three functions remove filters in different scopes, and picking the wrong one produces a number that's technically correct DAX but answers the wrong business question. ALL(Sales) removes every filter on the Sales table unconditionally, including the Europe report filter and the visual's own breakdown - so dividing by CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales)) always gives the true worldwide grand total, regardless of what's selected anywhere. ALLSELECTED() is different: it keeps filters applied outside the visual, so the Europe report-level filter stays active, and only removes the row/column filters generated by the visual itself, the category/year breakdown. That's what 'visual total' means: the total for everything the user actually selected, just not broken out by category and year. ALLEXCEPT(Sales, <columns to keep>) takes the opposite framing from ALL(Column) - instead of naming the few columns to clear, you name the few columns to keep filtered and everything else on that table gets cleared; written with no columns named to keep, ALLEXCEPT(Sales) behaves equivalently to ALL(Sales) for the grand-total case, so #3 and #1 should produce identical numbers. The real choice between ALL and ALLEXCEPT is about which list, to-clear or to-keep, is shorter and more readable for a given table, not a difference in what gets filtered when neither keeps any columns.
questions.professionalAnswer: Each of these clears filters at a different scope, and that's the whole ballgame here. The ALL version strips every filter off Sales entirely, Europe filter included, so its denominator is always the true worldwide total no matter what's selected on the page. ALLSELECTED is the one that respects the Europe filter - it only clears what the visual itself added, the category and year breakdown, so its denominator becomes the total for Europe specifically, which is what people usually mean by a 'visual total.' ALLEXCEPT, with no columns named to preserve, ends up doing the same thing as ALL in this case - it's really just a different way of writing 'clear everything,' useful when you'd rather list the columns to keep than the columns to clear. So #1 and #3 should match exactly, and #2 is the odd one out because it's the only one that respects the Europe selection.
questions.example: With the Europe filter active: the ALL-based measure's denominator is the worldwide total (ignores Europe); the ALLSELECTED-based measure's denominator is the Europe total (keeps the report filter, drops only category/year); the ALLEXCEPT(Sales)-based measure matches the ALL-based one since no columns are named to keep.
commonMistakes: Using ALL when the requirement is actually a 'visual total' that should respect report-level filters
Assuming ALLSELECTED clears all filters like ALL does
Thinking ALLEXCEPT and ALL always differ - with no columns named to keep, ALLEXCEPT(Table) behaves like ALL(Table)
Not checking which total the stakeholder actually wants (true grand total vs. respecting what they selected) before picking a function
keyPoints: ALL clears every filter unconditionally, including report-level filters
ALLSELECTED keeps filters set outside the visual, clears only the visual's own breakdown
ALLEXCEPT names columns to keep filtered; everything else on that table clears
ALLEXCEPT(Table) with nothing named to keep is equivalent to ALL(Table)
The business question - true grand total vs. visual/selected total - decides which function is correct

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ALL-based grand total measure
Correct ALLSELECTED-based visual total measure
Correct ALLEXCEPT equivalent and explanation of when it diverges from ALL
Clearly explains the business-question framing for choosing between them

questions.title: Indexed Views: Mechanics and Restrictions
questions.prompt: Explain how an indexed view actually works under the hood in SQL Server — what SQL Server materializes, how it keeps that materialized data in sync with the base tables, and why indexed views come with such a strict list of requirements (deterministic functions only, no outer joins, SCHEMABINDING, etc.).
questions.modelAnswer: A standard view is just a stored query — nothing is persisted, and every time you select from it, SQL Server substitutes the view's definition into your query and compiles a plan against the base tables. An indexed view is fundamentally different: when you create a unique clustered index on a view, SQL Server actually materializes the result set of that view's query onto disk, in exactly the structure a clustered index implies (a b-tree with the data at the leaf level, physically sorted by the clustered index key). From that point on, the view's rows exist as real, maintained data, not a re-run query. Once that materialized data exists, SQL Server has to keep it transactionally consistent with the base tables, so every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against the underlying tables also triggers maintenance of the indexed view's data as part of the same transaction — this is handled automatically and synchronously, which is why indexed views add write overhead in proportion to how many views depend on the table. The strict rules exist precisely because this maintenance has to be deterministic and unambiguous: SCHEMABINDING is required so the base tables can't be altered out from under the view's materialized structure; aggregate functions need COUNT_BIG rather than COUNT so NULL/overflow semantics are unambiguous; outer joins and subqueries are disallowed because the engine can't always determine, incrementally, exactly which materialized rows need to change when a base row changes; and non-deterministic functions (GETDATE(), RAND()) are banned because the materialized value has to be reproducible and tied only to its deterministic inputs. In short, an indexed view trades write-time cost and a narrow set of allowed constructs for read-time speed, because the expensive aggregation or join work is done once at write time instead of on every read.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about indexed views is that they flip a normal view inside out. A regular view is lazy — it's just a saved SELECT statement, and the actual work happens every time someone queries it. An indexed view is the opposite: the moment you put a unique clustered index on it, SQL Server goes and physically builds that result set on disk, like any other table, and from then on it has to maintain it in real time. So if you've got an indexed view that aggregates sales by product, every single insert or update to the Sales table also updates that materialized aggregate behind the scenes, inside the same transaction. That's the trade-off — you're paying extra cost on every write so that reads against the view are basically free, just reading pre-computed data off disk instead of re-aggregating millions of rows. The restrictions make total sense once you see it that way — SCHEMABINDING locks the base tables so nobody can change a column type underneath the materialized structure, you need COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT because the engine needs predictable, deterministic math to maintain the aggregate incrementally, and things like outer joins or non-deterministic functions like GETDATE() are blocked because the engine genuinely can't figure out, row by row, exactly how to patch the materialized result when something changes upstream. I'd tell an interviewer: use indexed views when you have an expensive aggregate that's read far more often than the base data is written — that's the sweet spot — and be honest that they're not free, they add real overhead to every write against the underlying tables.
commonMistakes: Thinking an indexed view is 'just a view with an index for faster lookup' rather than a materialized, physically stored structure
Forgetting that maintenance happens synchronously inside the write transaction, not as an async refresh job
Not knowing why COUNT_BIG is mandatory instead of COUNT or COUNT(*)
Assuming indexed views support the same join/subquery flexibility as regular views
Overusing indexed views on heavy-write tables without weighing the write-amplification cost
keyPoints: Indexed views physically materialize the result set via a unique clustered index
Base table DML synchronously maintains the indexed view's data in the same transaction
SCHEMABINDING prevents base table changes that would break the materialized structure
Deterministic-only functions and no outer joins/subqueries are required for unambiguous incremental maintenance
The performance trade-off is faster reads at the cost of slower writes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains physical materialization via unique clustered index
Explains synchronous maintenance on base table writes
Connects restrictions (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, no outer joins) to the underlying reason
Identifies the read-speed vs write-cost trade-off
Clarity and technical precision

questions.title: How Dynamic RLS Is Actually Enforced in the Service
questions.prompt: Explain, mechanically, how dynamic Row-Level Security is enforced end-to-end: what happens from the moment a user opens a published report in the Power BI Service to the moment their query returns filtered rows. Cover where USERPRINCIPALNAME() gets its value from, how roles map to users, and what changes when the semantic model sits behind a gateway versus a cloud-native source.
questions.modelAnswer: Dynamic RLS works by embedding a DAX filter expression on a table — commonly something like [EmailAddress] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() or a more complex expression using LOOKUPVALUE against a mapping table — inside a Role defined in the semantic model. That role is not tied to a specific user at definition time; instead, in the Service, workspace admins assign Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) users or security groups to that role through the dataset's security settings. When a user opens a report, the Service identifies the signed-in user's identity from their authenticated session, and that identity's UPN (user principal name, essentially their login email) is what USERPRINCIPALNAME() resolves to at query time. Critically, this resolution happens per-query, at the point the DAX engine (whether that's the Vertipaq in-memory engine for an Import model or the query pushed through DirectQuery) evaluates the role's filter expression — the engine effectively injects WHERE [EmailAddress] = '<the requesting user's UPN>' as a table filter before any visual's own filters are applied, and that filter propagates through the model's relationships exactly like any other filter would, which is why relationship direction and cross-filtering settings matter enormously for RLS correctness in more complex models. For an Import-mode semantic model, this filtering happens inside the Vertipaq engine in memory, entirely within the Service's own compute. When the model is DirectQuery and sits behind an on-premises data gateway, the mechanics change meaningfully: the Service still resolves the RLS filter expression, but it has to pass that filter down through the gateway into the native query sent to the source database — so the gateway is relaying a parameterized or literal filter as part of the generated SQL, and the enforcement point effectively shifts to query generation time rather than purely in-memory filtering. This is also why RLS with DirectQuery sources needs careful testing: if the gateway's generated SQL doesn't push the filter down correctly, or the data source doesn't support the pushed-down predicate efficiently, you can get both incorrect results and serious performance regressions compared to Import mode.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this as a chain of handoffs. It starts with a Role in the semantic model — that's where you write the actual DAX filter, like EmailAddress equals USERPRINCIPALNAME(), or something fancier that looks up the user in a separate security mapping table if you're doing group-based or hierarchical RLS. That role definition doesn't know about any specific person; it's generic. The person-to-role mapping happens separately, in the dataset security settings in the workspace, where an admin assigns actual Entra ID users or security groups to that role. Now, when someone opens the report, Power BI Service already knows who they are because they're authenticated through Entra ID — so it knows their UPN, basically their sign-in email. At query time, when the visual asks the model for data, the engine evaluates that role's DAX filter for the signed-in user, and USERPRINCIPALNAME() just resolves to that person's UPN right there. The engine effectively adds that filter onto the table before anything else runs, and because filters flow through relationships, if your model isn't set up carefully — wrong relationship direction, or RLS applied on the wrong side of a many-to-many — the filter might not reach every table you expect it to, which is a classic way dynamic RLS silently under- or over-filters data. Where it gets trickier is DirectQuery behind a gateway. With Import mode, all that filtering happens inside Vertipaq, Power BI's own in-memory engine, so it's fast and fully controlled by Power BI. With DirectQuery, Power BI has to translate that RLS filter into an actual predicate in the native SQL it sends through the gateway down to the source database — so now the gateway and the source database are both part of the enforcement chain, and if the generated query doesn't push the filter down cleanly, you can end up with wrong results or a query that's painfully slow because the filter isn't applied where it should be. That's exactly why I always test DirectQuery RLS with multiple test identities and actually check the generated SQL, not just trust that it works the same as Import.
commonMistakes: Assuming USERPRINCIPALNAME() is a stored value rather than resolved dynamically per query from the Service session
Not realizing role-to-user assignment happens in workspace dataset security settings, separate from the role's DAX definition
Forgetting that RLS filters propagate through relationships, so relationship direction/cross-filtering misconfigurations can break enforcement silently
Assuming DirectQuery RLS behaves identically to Import RLS, without accounting for gateway query pushdown
Failing to test RLS with 'View As Role' across multiple identities before publishing, especially with group-based mappings
keyPoints: Roles define a generic DAX filter; user/group-to-role assignment happens separately in Service dataset security
USERPRINCIPALNAME() resolves to the authenticated user's UPN at query time, not at role-authoring time
RLS filters propagate through model relationships, so direction and cross-filter settings affect correctness
Import mode enforces RLS inside Vertipaq in memory
DirectQuery RLS requires the filter to be pushed down into native SQL through the gateway, changing both correctness and performance characteristics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Role/DAX filter vs. Service-side user assignment separation
Correctly explains USERPRINCIPALNAME() resolution at query time
Explains filter propagation through relationships and its risks
Correctly contrasts Import-mode enforcement vs. DirectQuery/gateway pushdown
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Self-Hosted vs. Azure Integration Runtime: The Real Decision
questions.prompt: A client wants to copy data from an on-premises SQL Server database into Azure Data Lake using Data Factory. Explain what an Integration Runtime actually does in this pipeline, why a self-hosted IR is required here instead of the Azure IR, and how a managed identity and Key Vault fit into making this connection secure.
questions.modelAnswer: An Integration Runtime is the compute infrastructure Data Factory actually uses to execute activities — it's the thing that physically performs the data movement, dispatches transformation activities, and establishes network connections to data stores, rather than Data Factory's control plane doing any of that work directly. The Azure IR is fully managed, elastically scaled compute that Microsoft runs inside Azure's network; it can reach any data store that is reachable over the public internet or via private endpoints Data Factory itself can resolve, but it has no route into a private, on-premises network. A self-hosted IR is different: it's a piece of software you install yourself on a machine (or VM) that sits inside the same network as the on-premises SQL Server, and it works by making outbound-only connections back out to the Azure Data Factory service — it registers itself with your Data Factory instance and polls/receives work over that outbound channel, meaning you never have to open inbound ports into your on-prem network. In the described scenario, since the SQL Server lives on-premises with no public endpoint, the Azure IR has no network path to it at all, so a self-hosted IR installed inside (or with network access to) that on-prem environment is mandatory — it's what actually makes the TCP connection to SQL Server, pulls the data, and forwards it out to the cloud sink. On the security side, Managed Identity and Key Vault solve a different problem: avoiding hardcoded credentials in the pipeline's linked service definitions. Instead of storing a SQL login and password (or storage account keys) directly in the pipeline, Data Factory's system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity can be granted access to secrets stored in Azure Key Vault, and the Data Lake destination linked service can similarly authenticate via managed identity against Azure RBAC rather than a connection string with embedded keys. The self-hosted IR still needs to authenticate to the on-prem SQL Server using whatever credential that server requires (often still SQL auth or Windows auth, since on-prem doesn't recognize Azure managed identity), but that credential itself is pulled securely from Key Vault at runtime rather than being stored in plaintext in the pipeline definition, and the Data Lake side of the copy can go fully credential-less via managed identity and RBAC.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always explain Integration Runtime as the actual muscle behind Data Factory — the orchestration, scheduling, and pipeline definitions live in the Data Factory service, but the IR is what physically does the work of connecting to a data store and moving bytes. The Azure IR is Microsoft's own managed compute sitting inside Azure, which is great as long as everything you're touching is reachable from Azure's network — but it simply has no way to get into a private on-prem network, there's no route for it. That's exactly why, when the source is an on-prem SQL Server with no public endpoint, you need a self-hosted IR — it's software you install on a server inside that same network, and the clever bit is it only makes outbound calls back to Data Factory in Azure, so you're not opening any inbound firewall ports, which is usually a hard requirement for any client's network security team. Once that self-hosted IR is sitting there with a route to SQL Server, it's the one actually executing the copy activity — connecting to SQL Server, pulling rows, and streaming them out to whatever Azure sink you've configured, Data Lake in this case. Now, on the credentials side, I'd keep that completely separate from the IR question — that's about not wanting plaintext passwords sitting in your linked service JSON. Data Factory has its own managed identity, and I'd use that identity to pull the actual SQL Server credential out of Key Vault at runtime rather than typing it into the linked service directly — and for the Data Lake side, since that's all inside Azure, I can skip credentials almost entirely and just grant the Data Factory managed identity RBAC access directly on the storage account. So the self-hosted IR solves the 'how do I even reach this on-prem box' problem, and managed identity plus Key Vault solves the completely separate 'how do I avoid hardcoding secrets' problem — they're often asked about together but they're solving different layers of the same pipeline.
commonMistakes: Thinking Azure IR can reach on-premises resources if you just configure firewall rules, without needing a self-hosted IR
Confusing the Integration Runtime's job (executing data movement) with the Data Factory control plane's job (orchestration/scheduling)
Assuming self-hosted IR requires inbound firewall ports, when it actually only needs outbound connectivity
Believing managed identity alone can authenticate to an on-prem SQL Server the same way it does to Azure resources
Storing connection strings/passwords directly in linked services instead of referencing Key Vault secrets
keyPoints: The Integration Runtime is the actual compute that executes data movement/transformation, not the orchestration layer
Azure IR has no network route into private on-prem environments
Self-hosted IR runs inside the on-prem network and connects outbound-only to Data Factory
Managed identity + Key Vault eliminate hardcoded credentials in linked services
On-prem SQL Server authentication and Azure resource authentication are solved differently even in the same pipeline

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what an Integration Runtime does
Correctly explains why self-hosted IR is required for on-prem connectivity, including outbound-only networking
Correctly explains the managed identity + Key Vault role for secrets
Distinguishes the networking problem from the credentials problem
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Merge vs. Rebase on a Shared dbt Branch
questions.prompt: Two analysts are both working off the same feature branch that's several commits behind main, which has had conflicting SQL model changes merged in. Explain the mechanical difference between merging main into their branch versus rebasing their branch onto main, and why one of those choices is riskier on a branch other people are actively pulling from.
questions.modelAnswer: Merging main into a feature branch creates a new merge commit that has two parents — the tip of the feature branch and the tip of main — and it preserves the full existing history of both branches exactly as it happened; nothing is rewritten, commits keep their original hashes, and the merge commit simply records how the two histories were reconciled, including resolving the conflicting SQL model changes at that single point. Rebasing takes the opposite approach: it takes every commit that exists on the feature branch but not on main, and replays them one by one on top of main's current tip, as if the author had started their work from main's latest commit instead of the older one — each replayed commit gets a brand-new commit hash, because its parent has changed, even if the actual code diff is identical. This is the critical distinction for a shared branch: rebase rewrites commit history, which means every commit that existed before the rebase is effectively replaced by a new, different commit with the same changes but a different identity. If a second analyst has already pulled the old version of those commits and continues working on top of them, their local history and the rewritten remote history diverge completely — when they try to push or pull, Git sees what looks like two unrelated sets of commits sharing no common ancestor at the tip, and they'll either be forced to force-push over the rewritten history (destroying someone else's work) or do a confusing second merge/rebase to reconcile diverging duplicate commits. Merging avoids this entirely because it never rewrites what already exists — it only adds a new commit on top, so anyone who already has the old commits can pull the merge commit cleanly without any identity conflicts. The practical guidance that follows is: rebase is fine (and often preferred for a clean, linear history) on a branch only you are working on and haven't shared yet, but once a branch is shared and others are pulling from it, merging (or at minimum, coordinating the rebase with everyone who has a copy) is the safe choice.
questions.professionalAnswer: The simplest way I explain this is: merge adds, rebase rewrites. When you merge main into your feature branch, Git creates one new commit that has two parents — your branch's old tip and main's tip — and it resolves any conflicts right there in that single merge commit. Everything that existed before stays exactly as it was; you've just added something new on top that stitches the two histories together. Rebase does something fundamentally different — it takes your commits off their old starting point and replays them, one at a time, on top of wherever main currently is, and because each replayed commit now has a different parent, Git assigns it a brand-new hash even though the code change inside it might be identical to before. That's totally fine as long as you're the only person who has those commits. But the moment someone else has already pulled your original commits — say your teammate branched off your feature branch yesterday — and you go rebase and force-push, you've essentially replaced history they're already building on with an entirely different, same-looking-but-technically-distinct set of commits. When they try to sync up, Git doesn't see a clean continuation, it sees two diverging timelines, and they either end up force-pushing over your changes, or wrestling with duplicate-looking commits that don't actually match by hash. That's exactly the scenario here — with two analysts actively working off the same branch, I'd merge main in rather than rebase, resolve the SQL model conflicts in that one merge commit, and let everyone keep pulling cleanly. If I really wanted the cleaner linear history that rebase gives you, I'd only do that on a branch I know for certain nobody else has a copy of yet, and I'd be upfront with the team before force-pushing anything shared.
commonMistakes: Believing rebase and merge produce the same result just with a different-looking history
Not realizing rebased commits get entirely new hashes even when the diff content is unchanged
Force-pushing a rebased shared branch without coordinating with teammates who already have the old commits
Assuming merge commits are 'messier' and therefore always worse, without weighing the safety trade-off on shared branches
Confusing conflict resolution during rebase (resolved per replayed commit) with conflict resolution during merge (resolved once, in the merge commit)
keyPoints: Merge creates a new two-parent commit and preserves existing history unchanged
Rebase replays commits onto a new base, generating new hashes for every replayed commit
Rewriting history via rebase breaks shared branches because other copies no longer share commit identity
Merging is safe on shared/pulled branches because it never rewrites existing commits
Rebase is best reserved for local, unshared branches, or requires explicit team coordination

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains merge's two-parent, non-rewriting mechanics
Correctly explains rebase's replay-and-new-hash mechanics
Correctly identifies why rebase is risky specifically on a shared/already-pulled branch
Gives sound practical guidance on when each is appropriate
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: When a Snowflake Table Actually Needs an Explicit Clustering Key
questions.prompt: Explain how Snowflake's micro-partitioning and automatic clustering differ from a traditional B-tree index, what "natural clustering" means, and describe a concrete scenario on a multi-terabyte events table where you would define an explicit CLUSTER BY key versus one where you wouldn't bother.
questions.modelAnswer:
Snowflake automatically stores every table's data in immutable micro-partitions (roughly 50-500MB uncompressed each) and maintains metadata -- min/max values per column -- for every micro-partition. A query's WHERE clause is matched against that metadata to prune micro-partitions that can't contain matching rows, before any data is actually scanned. There's no index to build or maintain in the traditional B-tree sense; pruning is a property of how the data happens to be organized across micro-partitions, not a separate structure layered on top.

"Natural clustering" is simply however rows land in micro-partitions as a side effect of load/ingestion order. For an append-only, time-ordered load -- events arriving and being written roughly in timestamp order -- the table is often already well-clustered on the load date/timestamp column for free, with no explicit configuration at all.

An explicit CLUSTER BY key tells Snowflake's background automatic clustering service to continuously reorganize micro-partitions to keep rows with similar values of that key co-located -- and that reorganization costs ongoing compute credits. You'd define one where query patterns filter heavily on a column that is NOT correlated with insert order, on a table large and frequently-queried enough that the pruning gain clearly outweighs the reclustering cost -- e.g., a multi-TB events table ingested in timestamp order, where dashboards constantly filter WHERE customer_id = X and that column has no natural correlation to load time. You would NOT bother clustering if the table is already naturally well-clustered on the dominant filter column (e.g., filtering by event_date on a naturally time-ordered load), since reclustering an already-correlated column burns credits for no pruning benefit, or if the table is small enough that a full scan is already cheap regardless.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it: Snowflake doesn't really have indexes the way SQL Server does. It splits every table into micro-partitions automatically and keeps min/max metadata per column on each one, and pruning is just Snowflake skipping micro-partitions whose metadata can't match your WHERE clause. Nothing to build, nothing to maintain, by default.

"Natural clustering" is just what you get for free from load order -- if you're appending events roughly in timestamp order, the table's already pretty well organized by time without anyone doing anything.

Where I'd actually reach for an explicit CLUSTER BY key is when the dominant filter in my queries doesn't line up with how the data landed -- say a multi-TB events table loaded in timestamp order, but dashboards hammer it with customer_id filters all day. That's a real case for clustering, because Snowflake will keep reorganizing the data to keep each customer's rows together, which meaningfully helps pruning, and I'd check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION before and after to confirm it's actually helping. Where I wouldn't bother is clustering on a column that's already naturally correlated with load order -- like event_date on that same table -- because you'd just be paying ongoing reclustering credits for a benefit you already have for free.
commonMistakes: Treating CLUSTER BY like a free CREATE INDEX with no ongoing cost
Clustering on a column already naturally correlated with load order, wasting reclustering credits
Not checking SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION before and after committing to a clustering key
Assuming pruning requires some kind of index structure at all
Ignoring the ongoing background reclustering cost when deciding whether a key is worth it
keyPoints: Micro-partitions with min/max metadata enable pruning without any index structure
Natural clustering often comes for free from append/ingestion order
Explicit CLUSTER BY triggers paid, ongoing background reclustering
Best suited to large tables with high-cardinality filter columns uncorrelated with load order
Verify benefit with SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION rather than assuming

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the micro-partition pruning mechanism correctly
Explains natural clustering correctly
Identifies a correct scenario for an explicit CLUSTER BY key
Identifies a correct scenario where clustering is unnecessary
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: What Terraform State Actually Tracks, and Why Local State Breaks on a Team
questions.prompt: Explain what the Terraform state file (terraform.tfstate) actually stores beyond 'which resources exist,' and why two engineers running terraform apply against local state files for the same Azure data platform at the same time can corrupt the deployment even if their .tf code never conflicts.
questions.modelAnswer:
The state file is not just a list of resource names — it's a mapping from every resource block in the config to the real-world resource's provider-assigned ID, plus a full snapshot of every tracked attribute Terraform last saw for that resource (IDs, computed values, dependency ordering). That snapshot is what lets Terraform compute a diff on the next plan: it compares config, state, and real infrastructure as three separate things, not two.

With local state, each engineer has their own .tfstate file on their own machine, with no shared source of truth and no locking mechanism. If two engineers run apply around the same time, there's no serialization: each reads whatever state file it has locally, computes a plan against that potentially-stale snapshot, and writes changes back to its own local copy. One engineer's apply can create or modify a resource that the other engineer's stale state has no record of, so the next plan either tries to recreate something that already exists (erroring or duplicating billable resources) or tries to destroy/modify a resource whose state entry doesn't match reality anymore. This happens even if the .tf code itself never conflicts in version control, because the race is in the state file, not the code — which is exactly why a team setup needs a remote backend with locking, so applies against the same state are serialized and everyone reads/writes the same authoritative snapshot.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain it as: the state file isn't just 'these resources exist,' it's Terraform's record of exactly what it last saw for every resource — the real provider ID, every attribute, how things depend on each other. That's what plan actually diffs against, not just the .tf files.

The local-state problem is that each person's laptop has its own separate snapshot of that record, and nothing's coordinating writes to it. If I apply something and you apply something else around the same time, we're each working off our own possibly-stale copy, and whoever writes last just overwrites the other's state file — it doesn't merge, it clobbers. So now the state thinks a resource exists with one set of attributes, while in Azure it's actually something else, or doesn't exist, or exists twice. The .tf code can be perfectly clean and still produce that mess, because the collision isn't in the code at all, it's in two uncoordinated writes to the same tracking file. That's the whole reason remote state with locking exists — it makes applies take turns.
commonMistakes: Thinking the state file is just a resource inventory, not a snapshot of tracked attributes used for diffing
Assuming two engineers' .tf code being conflict-free means their applies are safe to run concurrently
Not realizing local state has no locking at all — a second apply doesn't wait, it just overwrites
Forgetting state can contain sensitive values (connection strings, keys) in plain text, which local unencrypted state exposes
Believing committing terraform.tfstate to git solves the team-sharing problem (it doesn't solve locking, and leaks secrets into history)
keyPoints: State maps config to real-world resource IDs and tracks every attribute Terraform last observed
Plan diffs against config, state, AND real infrastructure as three distinct sources
Local state has no locking, so concurrent applies race and the last write wins, clobbering the other's changes
The corruption happens even with conflict-free .tf code, because the race is in the state file
A remote backend with locking (e.g., azurerm storage with blob lease) serializes applies across a team

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what state tracks beyond existence
Explains why local state has no concurrency protection
Explains how this corrupts a deployment despite conflict-free code
Names remote state + locking as the fix

questions.title: Walking a Bill-of-Materials Hierarchy with a Recursive CTE
questions.prompt: AdventureWorks2012's Production.BillOfMaterials table models a bicycle's bill of materials: a top-level assembly (ProductAssemblyID) is built from component products (ComponentID), and some of those components are themselves sub-assemblies built from further components, to an unknown depth. Write a query that returns the full multi-level component tree for a given assembly, including each component's depth level, using only currently-active BOM rows. Then explain the two required parts of a recursive CTE, why one particular set operator is mandatory, and what safety valve you'd put in place before running this against unfamiliar data.
questions.modelAnswer:
A recursive CTE has exactly two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member that seeds the recursion (here, the direct components of the requested assembly), and a recursive member that references the CTE by its own name and joins the next level down onto the previous pass's results. SQL Server keeps re-executing the recursive member, feeding each pass's output back in as input to the next, until a pass produces zero new rows -- that's the only termination condition, which is exactly why cyclic data (a component that is, transitively, its own ancestor) can spin forever without a guard.

UNION ALL is mandatory, not a style choice: SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax does not permit plain UNION for the member union, because UNION's deduplication would have to compare against the full accumulated result set on every pass, which conflicts with how the recursive expansion is implemented. You also cannot put TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE itself inside the recursive member -- the recursive member is restricted to a simple SELECT...FROM CTE JOIN base-table shape.

The safety valve is OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on the outer statement. The default limit is 100 levels; set it explicitly (or to 0, meaning unlimited, only when you're certain the data is acyclic) so a bad BOM row with a circular reference fails fast with error 530 instead of running away. Finally, filter EndDate IS NULL in both the anchor and the recursive member's join predicate -- Production.BillOfMaterials keeps historical, retired component relationships, and without that filter the hierarchy walk includes assemblies that no longer apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a recursive CTE here because this is a classic parent-child walk of unknown depth -- you can't write a fixed number of self-joins when you don't know how many sub-assembly levels exist. I'd structure it as an anchor that grabs the direct components of the assembly I'm given, filtered to EndDate IS NULL so I'm not pulling in retired BOM relationships, starting at level zero. Then the recursive part joins BillOfMaterials back onto the CTE itself, matching the previous level's ComponentID to the new row's ProductAssemblyID, bumping the level each time. I always remind people UNION ALL isn't optional there -- SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax simply won't accept a plain UNION on that join. And before I'd run this against a BOM table I didn't already trust, I'd tack on OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100) or some sane number, because if there's ever a circular reference in that data -- a component that loops back to one of its own ancestors -- I want a clean error, not a query that just hangs.
questions.example:
WITH BOMHierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor: direct components of the requested assembly
    SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, 0 AS Level,
           CAST(ComponentID AS VARCHAR(400)) AS Path
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials
    WHERE ProductAssemblyID = 800 AND EndDate IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references BOMHierarchy by its own name
    SELECT bom.ProductAssemblyID, bom.ComponentID, bh.Level + 1,
           bh.Path + '/' + CAST(bom.ComponentID AS VARCHAR(20))
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials AS bom
    INNER JOIN BOMHierarchy AS bh
        ON bom.ProductAssemblyID = bh.ComponentID
    WHERE bom.EndDate IS NULL
)
SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, Level, Path
FROM BOMHierarchy
ORDER BY Level
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);
commonMistakes: Using UNION instead of UNION ALL, which T-SQL rejects for recursive CTEs
Forgetting to filter EndDate IS NULL, pulling in retired BOM relationships
Not setting MAXRECURSION, so a circular reference in the data hangs instead of erroring cleanly
Assuming the CTE itself is indexed or materialized, when it's really re-expanded pass by pass
Putting DISTINCT, TOP, or an outer join against the CTE inside the recursive member, which T-SQL disallows
keyPoints: Anchor member seeds the recursion; recursive member references the CTE by its own name
UNION ALL is required between anchor and recursive member -- plain UNION is disallowed
Recursion stops automatically when a pass produces zero new rows
OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) is the safety valve against circular/cyclic data
Filter EndDate IS NULL to exclude retired BOM relationships
The recursive member cannot contain TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct anchor/recursive member structure in the query
Explains why UNION ALL is mandatory, not a preference
Addresses recursion depth/cycle safety via MAXRECURSION
Filters to active BOM rows (EndDate IS NULL)
Correctly describes recursive CTE syntax restrictions
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Removing Duplicate Staging Rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
questions.prompt: A failed, partially-retried ETL load left Staging.SalesOrderDetail with duplicate rows sharing the same (SalesOrderID, ProductID), each with a different SalesOrderDetailID. Write a set-based query that deletes every duplicate except the one with the lowest SalesOrderDetailID for each key combination. Then explain why this approach is preferred over a cursor-based row-by-row deletion, and what would change in your query if you needed to keep the duplicate with the highest, rather than lowest, SalesOrderDetailID.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the right tool because it assigns a unique, strictly sequential number to every row within each partition without collapsing any rows the way GROUP BY would -- each duplicate row survives in the result set, just tagged with its position within its own (SalesOrderID, ProductID) group, ordered however I specify. Wrapping that in a CTE lets me then DELETE directly against the CTE wherever the assigned row number is greater than 1 -- SQL Server treats the CTE as a view onto the same underlying rows, so deleting from it deletes the real staging rows.

This beats a cursor for the same reason any row-by-row approach loses to a set-based one: a cursor would FETCH one row at a time, decide whether to delete it, and round-trip through the query engine's overhead for every single row -- on a staging table with any real volume, that's dramatically slower than a single set-based operation the engine can plan and execute as one pass (or a small number of passes) over the data, using whatever indexes exist on the partition/order columns.

To keep the highest SalesOrderDetailID instead of the lowest, the only change needed is the ORDER BY inside OVER(): ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC instead of ascending (or no direction, since ascending is the default) -- row number 1 then lands on the highest ID in each partition, and everything else (the PARTITION BY, the DELETE WHERE rn > 1) stays identical. It's worth noting RANK() or DENSE_RANK() would be the wrong choice here specifically because they assign the same rank to true ties -- I want exactly one designated "keeper" row per key no matter what, which is precisely what ROW_NUMBER()'s strict, no-ties-allowed numbering guarantees.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to reach for ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the duplicate key -- SalesOrderID and ProductID together -- ordered by SalesOrderDetailID ascending, so within each duplicate group the row I want to keep gets numbered 1 and everything else gets 2, 3, and so on. I put that inside a CTE, and then I can delete straight from the CTE wherever that row number is greater than one -- SQL Server lets you do that because the CTE is really just a lens onto the same underlying staging rows.

I'd explain to someone why I didn't write this as a cursor: a cursor processes one row at a time, and every one of those iterations carries its own overhead -- that's exactly the row-by-row anti-pattern this course warns about. SQL Server's engine is built to work on whole sets of rows at once, so a single set-based DELETE against the CTE lets the optimizer handle this as one efficient operation instead of forcing it into thousands of tiny ones.

And if someone asked me to flip it around and keep the highest ID instead of the lowest, that's a one-word change -- just add DESC to the ORDER BY inside the OVER() clause. I'd also mention I specifically didn't reach for RANK or DENSE_RANK here, because those can tie two rows at the same rank, and I need exactly one row designated as the keeper every time -- ROW_NUMBER is the only one of the three that guarantees that.
questions.example:
WITH Duplicates AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY SalesOrderID, ProductID
               ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Staging.SalesOrderDetail
)
DELETE FROM Duplicates
WHERE rn > 1;

-- To keep the HIGHEST SalesOrderDetailID instead, only the ORDER BY direction changes:
-- ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC
commonMistakes: Using a cursor or WHILE loop to delete duplicates row by row
Using RANK() or DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(), which can tie and leave more than one 'keeper' row
Forgetting that DELETE works against the CTE because it's a direct view onto the base rows, not a copy
Omitting an explicit ORDER BY inside OVER(), leaving which row survives undefined
Running the DELETE without first running the SELECT version to verify which rows would be removed
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) numbers every row without collapsing the result set
DELETE can run directly against a CTE wrapping the window function
Set-based deletion beats row-by-row cursor processing for performance at volume
ROW_NUMBER guarantees a single keeper per partition; RANK/DENSE_RANK do not
Flipping ASC/DESC in the ORDER BY changes which duplicate is kept

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ROW_NUMBER/PARTITION BY/DELETE query
Explains why set-based beats cursor-based deletion
Correctly identifies the ORDER BY change needed to keep the highest ID
Explains why ROW_NUMBER is preferred over RANK/DENSE_RANK here
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Covering, Filtered Index for a High-Frequency Reporting Query
questions.prompt: A reporting endpoint runs this query hundreds of times per minute: SELECT ProductID, Name, ListPrice FROM Production.Product WHERE Color = 'Red' AND SellEndDate IS NULL ORDER BY ListPrice. Design the single nonclustered index you'd create to best serve it -- specifying key column order, included columns, and any filter -- and explain exactly how you'd confirm in the execution plan that it's actually being used as a fully covering seek rather than falling back to a scan or a key lookup.
questions.modelAnswer:
The query filters on Color (equality) and SellEndDate IS NULL, then orders by ListPrice, and selects ProductID, Name, ListPrice. I'd build the index key on Color first, since it's the equality predicate the optimizer can seek on directly, then ListPrice second, since that both satisfies part of the ORDER BY and keeps rows pre-sorted within each color -- letting the engine potentially avoid a separate sort operator entirely. ProductID and Name don't belong in the key at all; they're only ever selected, never filtered or sorted on, so they belong as INCLUDE columns, which attaches their data to the index's leaf level without making them part of the search key (keeping the key itself narrow). Finally, since this query only ever cares about currently-active products, I'd add a filter: WHERE SellEndDate IS NULL, so the index only covers the subset of rows this specific query pattern actually needs -- smaller, faster to scan, and still perfectly usable by any other query matching that same filter condition.

To confirm it's working as intended, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run the exact production query. I'm looking for a single Index Seek operator with no accompanying Key Lookup and no separate Sort operator afterward -- that combination means the index is fully covering (every selected column came straight from the index, no trip back to the clustered index) and pre-sorted for the ORDER BY. If I instead see an Index Seek followed by a Key Lookup, that tells me I missed an included column the query actually needs. If I see a Sort operator after the seek, either my key column order doesn't match the ORDER BY the way I assumed, or the optimizer decided sorting was cheaper than using the index's physical order for some other reason. And if I see a Scan instead of a Seek at all, I'd first check that the filter predicate on the index exactly matches the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server will only use a filtered index when it can prove the query's predicate is a subset of the index's filter, and a subtle mismatch (like comparing against a variable instead of a literal in some SQL Server versions) can silently prevent that match and fall back to scanning the base table.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Walking through the query, I see one equality filter (Color), one IS NULL filter that's really describing 'currently active products' (SellEndDate), an ORDER BY on ListPrice, and three columns actually being selected. So my index key is Color first, because that's the equality predicate, then ListPrice second, because that handles the sort and keeps things grouped nicely within each color. ProductID and Name never show up in a WHERE or ORDER BY here, so I don't want them cluttering the key -- they go in as INCLUDE columns instead, just along for the ride so the index can hand back the full row without touching the base table. And since this query only ever wants active products, I'd make the whole index filtered on SellEndDate IS NULL -- there's no reason to carry the weight of retired products in an index built specifically for this access pattern.

To prove it's actually helping, I turn on the actual plan and run the real query, and I want to see exactly one operator: an Index Seek, nothing else hanging off it. If there's a Key Lookup tagging along, that tells me I forgot to include a column the query needed. If there's a Sort sitting after the seek, my key order isn't lining up with the ORDER BY the way I thought it would. And if I'm staring at a Scan instead of a Seek, my first suspicion is that the filter on the index doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server is strict about that match for a filtered index, and small mismatches are a classic reason the optimizer quietly falls back to ignoring it.
commonMistakes: Putting ProductID/Name in the index key instead of as INCLUDE columns, widening the key unnecessarily
Forgetting the ORDER BY column when choosing key column order, leaving a Sort in the plan
Leaving off the filter, indexing retired products the query never actually needs
Assuming an Index Seek alone proves full coverage without checking for an accompanying Key Lookup
Writing a filter predicate that doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause, causing SQL Server to ignore the filtered index
keyPoints: Equality predicate columns go first in the index key, ahead of sort/range columns
ORDER BY columns in the key can eliminate a separate Sort operator
Select-only columns belong in INCLUDE, not the key, to keep the key narrow
A filtered index should match the query's WHERE clause as closely as possible
Verify with the actual execution plan: single seek, no Key Lookup, no Sort = fully covering

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct key column choice and order (Color, ListPrice)
Correctly places ProductID/Name as INCLUDE columns
Correctly applies the SellEndDate IS NULL filter
Describes verifying via actual execution plan (seek, no key lookup, no sort)
Explains what a Key Lookup or Sort in the plan would each indicate is wrong
