questions.title: Writing a Revenue Measure That Plain SUM Can't Express
questions.prompt: Sales[Quantity] and Sales[UnitPrice] exist as separate columns, but there's no stored Revenue column. Write a measure that totals revenue, filtered to only rows where the related SalesTerritory[Country] isn't the United States, and explain why SUM alone cannot do this.
questions.code:
Non-USA Revenue =
SUMX(
    FILTER(
        Sales,
        RELATED(SalesTerritory[Country]) <> "United States"
    ),
    Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]
)
questions.modelAnswer: Plain SUM only aggregates a single existing column directly - it has nothing to point at here, because revenue is a per-row computation (Quantity times UnitPrice), not a stored value. SUMX is an iterator: it walks the table row by row, evaluates an expression using that row's own values, then adds up the results - exactly what's needed to compute Quantity times UnitPrice fresh for each row before summing. Combining SUMX with FILTER handles the country condition: FILTER returns the subset of Sales rows where the related country isn't 'United States,' reached via RELATED since Country lives on the territory table, and SUMX then iterates only that filtered subset rather than the whole table. SUM alone can express neither the per-row multiplication nor the conditional subset - both require row-by-row evaluation, which is the entire reason the X-suffixed iterator functions exist.
questions.professionalAnswer: SUM can only point at a single column that already exists, and revenue here doesn't exist as a column - it only exists as Quantity times UnitPrice computed per row. That's exactly what SUMX is for: it goes row by row, computes that multiplication fresh each time, and adds the results together. To handle the country exclusion, I'd wrap the table argument in a FILTER that uses RELATED to reach the territory table's Country column from each Sales row, and SUMX then only iterates over the rows that pass. There's really no way to get SUM to do either of those two things - the per-row math or the conditional subset - because SUM was never built to evaluate an expression, only to add up a column that's already there.
questions.example: Contrast: Total Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) with no FILTER would total revenue across every country; adding the FILTER narrows the exact rows SUMX iterates.
commonMistakes: Trying to write SUM(Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) directly - SUM doesn't accept an expression, only a single column
Forgetting RELATED is needed to reach the country column on a different table from inside the row-by-row FILTER condition
Not realizing FILTER's second argument is itself evaluated in row context per row of Sales
Using a calculated column instead of a measure, pre-computing per-row revenue and losing the ability to recompute dynamically under different filter contexts
keyPoints: SUMX evaluates an expression row by row, then sums the results
Use SUMX whenever the needed value isn't a single stored column
FILTER inside SUMX's table argument narrows which rows get iterated
RELATED reaches a related table's column from inside row context

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct SUMX + FILTER + RELATED expression
Explains why SUM alone cannot express this
Explains the role of FILTER narrowing the iterated rows
Explains RELATED's role in reaching the related table

questions.title: Rewriting a YoY Growth Measure With Variables
questions.prompt: Rewrite this measure to follow DAX best practices, and explain each change: Sales YoY Growth % = ([Sales] - CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD('Date'[Date], -12, MONTH))) / CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD('Date'[Date], -12, MONTH))
questions.code:
Sales YoY Growth %% =
VAR SalesPriorYear =
    CALCULATE ( [Sales], PARALLELPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], -12, MONTH ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( [Sales] - SalesPriorYear, SalesPriorYear )
questions.modelAnswer: Two problems, two fixes. First, CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD(...)) is written twice and evaluated twice - identical work done over again for no reason, which costs real query time on a large model. A VAR computes it once, names it, and both places that need it reference the stored result instead of recomputing it, roughly halving the work for this formula. Second, the plain '/' operator throws an error the instant the denominator is zero or blank, which happens for any period with no prior-year data - a new product line, a new store, the first year of history - and that error surfaces to end users as a broken visual instead of a clean blank. DIVIDE handles a zero/blank denominator gracefully, returning blank by default, or a value you specify, instead of erroring. Naming the variable SalesPriorYear also makes the RETURN line read as plain English instead of a repeated formula, which matters when someone else, or you in six months, has to maintain this.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two things jump out. The same CALCULATE/PARALLELPERIOD expression is written twice, which means the engine computes 'sales a year ago' twice for no reason - I'd pull that into a VAR, compute it once, and reference it in both places it's needed, which is real query-time savings, not just tidiness. The other issue is the plain division - the moment there's no prior-year data at all, which happens for anything new, that divide-by-zero throws an error straight into the visual instead of quietly returning blank. I'd swap it for DIVIDE, which handles that gracefully. On top of the performance and correctness fixes, naming the variable SalesPriorYear also just makes the RETURN line readable as a sentence instead of a repeated formula, which matters for anyone maintaining this later, including me.
questions.example: Debugging tip from the same pattern: temporarily change RETURN to just SalesPriorYear to inspect what the variable actually holds for a given filter context, before reinstating the real DIVIDE expression.
commonMistakes: Leaving the repeated CALCULATE/PARALLELPERIOD expression evaluated twice instead of once via a variable
Using plain division and letting the report error out on periods with no prior-year data
Naming variables generically (Var1, Result) instead of something that documents what the value represents
Not knowing the VAR-swap-to-RETURN trick for isolating which part of a formula produces an unexpected value
keyPoints: VAR/RETURN computes a repeated subexpression once instead of multiple times
DIVIDE avoids division-by-zero/blank errors that plain / throws
Named variables double as self-documentation
Temporarily returning a variable directly is a fast debugging technique

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct VAR/RETURN rewrite eliminating the duplicated CALCULATE call
Correct use of DIVIDE in place of /
Explains the performance benefit of computing once vs twice
Explains the zero/blank-denominator failure mode DIVIDE avoids

questions.title: Fix the Non-SARGable Order Lookup
questions.prompt: The query below is used in a nightly dashboard refresh and is now the slowest query in the job, taking almost 4 minutes against the Orders table (60M rows, nonclustered index on OrderDate). Rewrite it so it can use an index seek instead of a scan, without changing what it returns.
questions.code:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) = '2026-03-15'
   OR DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) = '2026-03-16';
questions.modelAnswer: This query has two separate non-SARGable predicates combined with OR, each of which independently forces a full scan: CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) wraps the column in a string conversion before comparing it, and DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) performs arithmetic on the column before comparing it — both require per-row evaluation across all 60 million rows, and the OR compounds the cost further because the optimizer can't cleanly combine two non-seekable branches into a single seek plan. Both predicates are actually expressing the exact same intent (rows where OrderDate falls on March 15, 2026), so the correct fix is to collapse them into a single SARGable range predicate that leaves OrderDate bare on one side of the comparison, using a half-open interval to correctly capture the entire day regardless of time-of-day values stored in the column.
questions.professionalAnswer: Looking at this, both of these predicates are just two different, overcomplicated ways of saying 'OrderDate is March 15th, 2026' — one converts the column to a string and compares it to a string literal, the other adds a day and compares to the 16th, and both of those operations have to run against the column before SQL Server can even check the condition, which means it can't seek, it has to scan every row and compute the expression first. I'd collapse this down to a plain date range using the raw column, written as a half-open interval so it still works correctly even if OrderDate has a time component — that keeps the column bare on the left side of the comparison so the optimizer can seek straight into the nonclustered index on OrderDate instead of touching all 60 million rows.
questions.example:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-03-15'
  AND OrderDate < '2026-03-16';
commonMistakes: Only fixing one of the two predicates and leaving the other non-SARGable branch in the OR
Using OrderDate = '2026-03-15' directly, which silently misses rows with a non-midnight time component
Not recognizing that both predicates express the same logical condition and can be merged into one range
Adding an index hint instead of fixing the predicate, which doesn't solve the underlying non-SARGable issue
Forgetting the half-open interval pattern and using BETWEEN with an inclusive end date/time that can miss late-day rows
keyPoints: Both original predicates wrap the column in a function/arithmetic, forcing per-row evaluation and a scan
Recognize that both branches express the same underlying date condition
Rewrite as a single SARGable half-open range on the bare column
Half-open range correctly handles any time-of-day component on OrderDate
Resulting plan should allow an index seek on the nonclustered OrderDate index

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies both predicates as non-SARGable and explains why
Produces a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Uses a half-open interval that correctly handles time components
Explains expected improvement (seek vs scan)
Clean, correct SQL syntax

questions.title: Fix the Broken YTD Measure
questions.prompt: A YTD Sales measure is returning the same value for every month in a line chart instead of accumulating within each year. The model has a proper marked date table (Dates[Date]) related to Sales[OrderDate]. Diagnose and fix the DAX below.
questions.modelAnswer: The bug is that DATESYTD is being pointed at Sales[OrderDate] instead of the marked date table's date column, Dates[Date]. DATESYTD requires a contiguous, single-column date reference from a properly marked date table in order to correctly generate the set of dates from the start of the year up through the latest date in the current filter context — when you give it a column from a fact table like Sales[OrderDate], the function either errors in stricter scenarios or, if it technically runs, fails to produce the correct year-to-date date range because it isn't operating against the marked date dimension that the model's time intelligence relies on, which is why the result ends up static/incorrect across the visual rather than accumulating per period. The fix is to reference Dates[Date] (the date table's column) inside DATESYTD, relying on the active relationship between Dates[Date] and Sales[OrderDate] to propagate the resulting date filter onto the Sales table through normal filter propagation, exactly the way all of Power BI's built-in time intelligence functions expect to be used.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I see DATESYTD referencing a column straight off the fact table rather than the date table, that's the bug. Time intelligence functions like DATESYTD are built to work against a proper, contiguous date dimension — they need to generate the full date range from January 1st up to the current context's latest date, and they do that correctly only when pointed at the marked date table's date column. Pointing it at Sales[OrderDate] instead means it's not working with the dimension the model's time intelligence is built around, so instead of correctly expanding to 'every day from the start of this year through now,' it's not producing the right filtered date set at all, which is exactly why you're seeing the same number repeat across every month instead of accumulating. The fix is just to swap the reference to Dates[Date], and let the existing relationship between Dates[Date] and Sales[OrderDate] do its job of pushing that date filter down onto the Sales table like it would for any other filter.
questions.example:
YTD Sales =
CALCULATE(
    SUM(Sales[Amount]),
    DATESYTD(Dates[Date])
)
-- Dates[Date] must come from a table marked as the Date Table
-- in Power BI, with an active relationship to Sales[OrderDate].
commonMistakes: Referencing the fact table's date column instead of the marked date table's column inside time intelligence functions
Forgetting to actually mark the Dates table as a 'Date Table' in Model view, even if the column reference is fixed
Assuming a relationship alone (without 'Mark as Date Table') is sufficient for DATESYTD to work correctly
Not checking that the date table is contiguous (no missing calendar days) which DATESYTD also requires
Confusing DATESYTD's date range output with a value, forgetting it must be wrapped in CALCULATE with an aggregate
keyPoints: DATESYTD must reference the marked date table's column, not a fact table date column
The date table must be marked as a Date Table and be contiguous for correct results
Filter propagation from Dates[Date] to Sales[OrderDate] relies on the active relationship
CALCULATE wraps the aggregate while DATESYTD supplies the filtered date range
Symptom (flat/repeated values) is a strong signal of a broken time-intelligence date reference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the root cause (wrong column reference)
Provides the correct fixed DAX
Explains the requirement for a marked, contiguous date table
Explains filter propagation via the relationship
Clarity

questions.title: Design a Tumbling Window Pipeline With Retry and Alerting
questions.prompt: You need an Azure Data Factory pipeline that ingests hourly batch files from a partner into Azure Data Lake, processes each hour's file exactly once even if the pipeline is paused and resumed, and alerts the team on repeated failure without manual babysitting. Describe the trigger type, retry configuration, and failure-handling pattern you'd configure, and explain why a tumbling window trigger is the right choice over a simple schedule trigger here.
questions.modelAnswer: A tumbling window trigger is the correct choice because it is explicitly designed around fixed, non-overlapping time windows that each get their own tracked execution state and window start/end time (@trigger().outputs.windowStartTime / windowEndTime), which lets the pipeline know precisely which hour's file it should be processing for that run, and critically, it supports dependency and retry semantics plus automatic backfill: if the pipeline is paused for several hours and then resumed, the tumbling window trigger will automatically queue and execute the missed windows in order, each exactly once, rather than simply skipping ahead to 'now' the way a plain schedule trigger would. A schedule trigger fires at wall-clock times with no concept of windows or backfill — if it's paused, those fire times are simply lost, and there's no built-in mechanism tying a given run to 'which hour's file' beyond what you manually derive from the trigger time, making exactly-once-per-hour semantics much harder to guarantee. For retry, I'd configure the trigger's own retryPolicy (count and interval) for transient failures at the trigger level, and additionally configure the Copy Activity's own retry count/interval for transient source/sink connectivity issues, since activity-level retries handle smaller transient hiccups without re-running the entire pipeline. For failure handling and alerting, I'd attach a failure-path activity (via the 'on failure' dependency condition in the pipeline canvas) that runs after the main activities only if they fail, which calls a Logic App or Azure Function to post to Teams/email, or more directly, configure an Azure Monitor alert rule on the Data Factory's own PipelineFailedRuns metric so the team gets paged without needing custom alerting logic embedded in every pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a tumbling window trigger here specifically because of the backfill and exactly-once guarantees it gives you, which a plain schedule trigger just doesn't have. A schedule trigger is basically a clock — it fires at set wall-clock times, and if the pipeline's paused when a fire time comes around, that execution is just gone, there's no catch-up. A tumbling window trigger instead tracks discrete time windows, each with its own state, so if I pause it for six hours and then resume, it knows exactly which windows it missed and it'll queue them up and run them in order, each one exactly once — which is exactly the 'process each hour's file exactly once even after a pause' requirement here. Inside the pipeline, I'd use the trigger's own windowStartTime and windowEndTime parameters to construct the exact filename or path for that hour's partner file, so there's no ambiguity about which window a given run corresponds to. For retries, I'd set them at two levels — a retry policy on the trigger itself for the pipeline as a whole, and separately a retry count on the Copy Activity itself, since a lot of these partner-file failures are transient network blips that resolve themselves on a quick retry without needing to escalate. And for the 'alert without babysitting' part, I wouldn't build custom alerting logic inside the pipeline — I'd set an Azure Monitor alert rule directly against Data Factory's pipeline failure metrics, so once retries are exhausted and a run is truly failed, it pages the team through whatever channel they already use, rather than relying on someone checking the monitoring tab.
commonMistakes: Choosing a schedule trigger and manually trying to reconstruct 'which hour' logic from current wall-clock time
Assuming a paused schedule trigger will automatically backfill missed runs the way a tumbling window trigger does
Only configuring retries at the activity level and ignoring trigger-level retry policy, or vice versa
Building custom email/Teams alerting inside every pipeline instead of using Azure Monitor alert rules on Data Factory metrics
Not using windowStartTime/windowEndTime to deterministically identify which file/partition a given run should process
keyPoints: Tumbling window trigger tracks discrete, stateful time windows with automatic backfill on resume
windowStartTime/windowEndTime deterministically identify which hour's data a run should process
Retry should be configured at both the trigger level and the activity level for different failure classes
Azure Monitor alert rules on Data Factory metrics provide alerting without custom in-pipeline logic
Schedule triggers lack windowing/backfill semantics, making exactly-once-per-period harder to guarantee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly justifies tumbling window trigger over schedule trigger with backfill/windowing reasoning
Correctly describes retry configuration at trigger and activity levels
Correctly describes a sound failure-alerting pattern
Uses windowStartTime/windowEndTime correctly to identify the processing window
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Writing an Incremental dbt Model With the merge Strategy
questions.prompt: Write a dbt model (models/marts/fct_orders.sql) that incrementally loads from a staging model stg_orders using the merge incremental strategy, keyed on order_id, that only processes rows with updated_at newer than the max already loaded, and is safe to run with --full-refresh. Then explain what is_incremental() does and why wrapping the filter in that macro matters.
questions.modelAnswer:
The config block sets materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id', and incremental_strategy='merge'. The filter against already-loaded data is wrapped in {% if is_incremental() %} ... {% endif %}, comparing stg_orders.updated_at to the max already in the target: (select max(updated_at) from {{ this }}).

is_incremental() returns true only when the model already exists as a table in the target AND the current invocation is not a full refresh. On a genuine first run, or any run with --full-refresh, dbt drops and rebuilds the table from scratch, so the entire is_incremental() block is skipped and the model simply selects every row from stg_orders with no filter at all.

That's exactly why wrapping the filter in the conditional is what makes the model safe to full-refresh: without the guard, a full-refresh run would try to query {{ this }} to find the max already-loaded updated_at before the table exists (or before it's been rebuilt), which either errors outright or references stale data. Querying {{ this }} is only safe, and only meaningful, inside the is_incremental() block.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd set this up with materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id', incremental_strategy='merge' in the config block, then write the base select against stg_orders, and wrap the "only new stuff" filter in an is_incremental() block that compares updated_at against the max already sitting in {{ this }}.

The reason that guard matters: is_incremental() is only true when the table already exists and we're not doing a full refresh. The first time this ever runs, or any time someone runs --full-refresh, dbt just rebuilds the whole table, so that block gets skipped entirely and the model pulls everything. If I didn't wrap the filter in that check, a full-refresh run would try to select max(updated_at) from a table that either doesn't exist yet or is about to be dropped and rebuilt -- that's exactly the kind of thing that breaks a model the first time someone runs it in a new environment.
commonMistakes: Forgetting unique_key, causing merge to behave like plain appends with duplicate inserts
Querying {{ this }} outside the is_incremental() guard, breaking full-refresh and first runs
Hardcoding the target table name instead of using {{ this }}, breaking across environments
Forgetting to set materialized='incremental' in the config block
Not accounting for the very first run, when the table doesn't exist yet
keyPoints: Config block sets materialized/unique_key/incremental_strategy
is_incremental() is true only on existing, non-full-refresh runs
Wrapping the filter in is_incremental() is what keeps the model safe for full-refresh
{{ this }} refers to the model's own already-built target table
merge requires unique_key to perform correct upsert semantics

Correct is_incremental() usage and filter
Explains why this keeps the model safe for full-refresh
Explains unique_key's role in merge

questions.title: Deploying Azure SQL with Bicep, and What a Missing Default Parameter Does in CI/CD
questions.prompt: Write a Bicep template that deploys an Azure SQL logical server, a database on that server, and a firewall rule allowing Azure services to connect, using parameters for the server name, admin login, admin password, database SKU, and the firewall rule's IP range. Then explain the real difference between a Bicep parameter declared with a default value and one declared without a default, specifically in terms of what happens when that template is deployed non-interactively from a CI/CD pipeline.
questions.modelAnswer:
A Bicep parameter declared with a default value is optional at deployment time: if the caller, whether that's a CI/CD pipeline, an az deployment command, or another module, doesn't explicitly supply a value, Bicep silently falls back to the default and the deployment proceeds without complaint. A parameter declared without a default is required: Bicep/ARM validates that every required parameter has a supplied value before the deployment is even allowed to start, and if one is missing, the deployment fails immediately at validation with an explicit 'missing required parameter' error.

That distinction matters most for a non-interactive CI/CD pipeline, because there's no human sitting at a prompt to supply a forgotten value -- whatever behavior the parameter declaration specifies is exactly what happens, with zero chance for someone to notice and type in a correction partway through. For a value like location or databaseSku, where there's a sensible standard choice most deployments should use, a default is appropriate: it lets most pipeline runs omit it entirely while still allowing an override when a specific deployment genuinely needs one. For sqlAdminLogin and especially sqlAdminPassword, the opposite is true: those should be required parameters with no default (the password additionally marked @secure() so it's never persisted in deployment history or logs), precisely because you want a hard, explicit failure forcing the pipeline to pull the value from a key vault or secure variable group every single time, rather than risk a template silently deploying with some hardcoded or forgotten placeholder credential baked into source control.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd put it: a default value makes a parameter optional, no default makes it mandatory, and the difference only really bites once nobody's around to catch a mistake -- which is exactly the situation in a CI/CD pipeline. If a parameter has a default and the pipeline doesn't pass anything for it, the deployment just quietly uses that default and keeps going. If there's no default and the pipeline forgets to pass it, the deployment refuses to even start -- it fails validation up front with a clear error instead of limping along with some guessed value.

That's why I'm deliberate about which of my parameters get defaults. Something like location or the database SKU, where there's a perfectly reasonable standard choice -- sure, give it a default, so most runs don't even have to think about it but can still override it when they need to. But the admin login and especially the admin password -- those I leave without defaults on purpose, and I mark the password @secure() on top of that. I want the pipeline to be forced to pull that value from somewhere secure every time, not accidentally succeed with a stale or hardcoded credential nobody noticed was still sitting there as a fallback.
commonMistakes: Giving sqlAdminPassword a default value (even a blank placeholder), undermining the point of requiring it explicitly each deployment
Forgetting the @secure() decorator on the password parameter, exposing it in deployment history
Using an overly broad firewall IP range instead of the 0.0.0.0-0.0.0.0 'Allow Azure services' convention
Hardcoding the database SKU instead of exposing it as a parameter
Assuming a parameter with a default still forces the pipeline to supply a value
keyPoints: A defaulted parameter is optional; the deployment silently falls back to the default if omitted
A non-defaulted parameter is required; validation fails immediately if it's missing
In non-interactive CI/CD, there's no prompt to recover from a missing required value -- it simply fails fast
Secrets like the admin password should be required (no default) and marked @secure()
Standard, non-sensitive values like location or SKU are reasonable candidates for defaults

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Bicep resources (SQL server, database, firewall rule)
Correct parameterization of server name, admin login/password, SKU, and IP range
Correct @secure() usage on the password parameter
Accurately explains optional-vs-required parameter behavior at deployment time
Explains why secrets should never have defaults in a CI/CD context

questions.title: Writing a Reusable Terraform Module for an Event Hub Namespace
questions.prompt: Write a reusable Terraform module (not a root module) that provisions an Azure Event Hub Namespace and one Event Hub inside it, parameterized by environment so throughput units and the namespace SKU differ between dev and prod, and that outputs the Event Hub's connection string for a downstream ingestion pipeline to consume. What's the risk of outputting that connection string the naive way, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer:
The module takes a variable like environment (validated to "dev" or "prod") and uses a lookup map keyed on that variable to pick sku and capacity, rather than hardcoding two near-duplicate resource blocks. azurerm_eventhub_namespace takes those as inputs; azurerm_eventhub nests under it with partition_count and message_retention; an azurerm_eventhub_authorization_rule (or a namespace-level rule) is what actually has listen/send permissions and exposes primary_connection_string.

The risk of a naive `output "connection_string" { value = azurerm_eventhub_authorization_rule.this.primary_connection_string }` is that Terraform prints outputs to the console on every apply/plan by default and writes the raw value into the state file in plain text — anyone with state access or plan output in CI logs now has a live credential. The fix has two parts: mark the output `sensitive = true` so it's redacted from CLI output (this does NOT encrypt it in state, it only hides console printing), and for the real fix, don't output the raw secret at all — write it into an azurerm_key_vault_secret resource instead, and have the downstream pipeline read the secret from Key Vault at runtime rather than receiving it as a Terraform output. That also means rotating the key doesn't require a new apply/output to propagate.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd structure it as a standalone module folder with variables.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf. The environment variable drives a lookup map for SKU and throughput units so I'm not duplicating the resource block twice — one azurerm_eventhub_namespace, one azurerm_eventhub nested under it, plus an authorization rule for the connection string.

On the output — if I just output primary_connection_string directly, that's a live credential sitting in plain text in the state file and printed to the terminal on every apply unless I mark it sensitive. Marking it sensitive stops it from printing to the console, but it's still sitting unencrypted in state, so that's not actually a fix, just hiding the symptom. What I'd really do is skip outputting the raw secret entirely — push it into Key Vault as a secret resource from the module, and have the pipeline pull it from Key Vault at runtime instead of getting it handed to it as a Terraform output.
commonMistakes: Duplicating near-identical resource blocks per environment instead of parameterizing with a variable and lookup map
Outputting a connection string without marking it sensitive, leaking it into CLI/CI logs
Believing sensitive = true encrypts the value in state, when it only redacts console output
Hardcoding partition count/retention instead of exposing them as variables for reuse across event hubs
Forgetting the authorization rule is a separate resource from the namespace/event hub and omitting it entirely
keyPoints: Module is parameterized by environment via a variable with validation, not duplicated per environment
A lookup map keyed on environment drives SKU/capacity differences
The connection string lives on an authorization rule resource, not the namespace or event hub directly
sensitive = true only hides console output; state still holds the raw value in plain text
The real fix routes the secret through Key Vault instead of handing it to the pipeline as a raw output

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct module structure and resource blocks
Correctly parameterizes by environment without duplication
Identifies the plaintext-in-state risk of the raw output
Proposes Key Vault (or equivalent) as the real fix, not just sensitive = true

questions.title: Creating a Resource Monitor to Cap a Runaway Warehouse Before It Burns the Month's Credits
questions.prompt: Write the SQL to create a Snowflake resource monitor named MONTHLY_ETL_MONITOR with a 5000-credit monthly quota that notifies account admins at 75% and suspends new statements (letting already-running queries finish) at 100%, then assign it to a warehouse called ETL_WH. Explain the difference between the SUSPEND and SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY triggers and which one actually belongs on this warehouse.
questions.modelAnswer:
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR takes a CREDIT_QUOTA, a FREQUENCY (MONTHLY here), a START_TIMESTAMP, and a list of TRIGGERS, each pairing a percentage with an action: NOTIFY just emails/alerts account admins with no effect on the warehouse; SUSPEND stops the warehouse from accepting new statements but lets anything already executing finish to completion; SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY cancels all running queries right away, full stop. The monitor is attached to a warehouse with ALTER WAREHOUSE ... SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = ...

For ETL_WH specifically, SUSPEND is the right trigger at 100%, not SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY: an ETL warehouse is typically mid-way through multi-statement loads or MERGE operations when a quota is hit, and SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY killing those mid-transaction risks partial writes or forces a rerun from scratch, whereas SUSPEND just stops anything new from starting while letting in-flight work finish cleanly. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY is better reserved as a true emergency backstop — often configured as a second trigger at something like 110% — for genuine runaway scenarios where letting anything else finish isn't acceptable.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd create the monitor with the quota and frequency, add a 75% NOTIFY trigger so admins get warned before anything happens operationally, and a 100% SUSPEND trigger — then attach it to the warehouse with an ALTER WAREHOUSE statement.

On SUSPEND vs SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY — SUSPEND just stops new queries from starting but lets whatever's already running finish, while SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY kills everything in flight right now. For an ETL warehouse, I want SUSPEND at 100%, because that warehouse is probably in the middle of a multi-step load, and I'd much rather let that finish cleanly than cancel it mid-write and have to figure out what state it left things in. I'd think about SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY as a second, higher trigger — like 110% — as a genuine last-resort hard stop, not the normal 100% behavior.
questions.example:
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR monthly_etl_monitor
  WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 5000
  FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
  START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS
    ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
    ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND
    ON 110 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY;

ALTER WAREHOUSE etl_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = monthly_etl_monitor;
commonMistakes: Assuming SUSPEND cancels currently running queries, when it only blocks new ones from starting
Setting SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY as the normal 100% action on a warehouse running multi-step writes, risking partial/incomplete loads
Forgetting that a NOTIFY-only trigger has zero effect on the warehouse itself — it's purely an alert
Not setting any hard backstop trigger, relying entirely on someone reading the 75% notification in time
Forgetting the monitor has to be explicitly assigned to the warehouse with ALTER WAREHOUSE after creation
keyPoints: CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR needs a CREDIT_QUOTA, FREQUENCY, and TRIGGERS with percentage + action pairs
NOTIFY alerts only; SUSPEND blocks new statements but lets running ones finish; SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY cancels everything now
The monitor must be attached to the warehouse separately via ALTER WAREHOUSE ... SET RESOURCE_MONITOR
SUSPEND is the right 100% action for an ETL warehouse to avoid killing in-flight multi-step loads
SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY is best used as a secondary, higher-threshold hard stop, not the default ceiling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR syntax with quota/frequency/triggers
Correctly attaches the monitor to the warehouse
Correctly distinguishes SUSPEND vs SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY
Justifies SUSPEND (not SUSPEND_IMMEDIATELY) for an ETL warehouse

questions.title: Setting Up Snowpipe Auto-Ingest, and Proving to Yourself the Files Are Actually Loading
questions.prompt: Write the SQL to create a Snowpipe named RAW_EVENTS_PIPE that auto-ingests new JSON files landing in an external stage into a RAW_EVENTS table. A week after go-live, files are visibly landing in the stage but rows aren't showing up in the table. Walk through exactly which Snowflake objects/functions you'd query, in order, to find out why — and the two most common root causes you'd expect to find.
questions.modelAnswer:
CREATE PIPE with AUTO_INGEST = TRUE wraps a COPY INTO statement; the pipe itself doesn't poll the stage — it relies on a cloud storage event notification (an SNS topic on S3, Event Grid on Azure, Pub/Sub on GCS) that's configured separately to notify Snowflake's internal queue whenever a new file lands.

To diagnose rows not appearing despite files landing, I'd check, in order: first, SELECT SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS('RAW_EVENTS_PIPE') to see the pipe's execution state, pendingFileCount, and lastIngestedTimestamp — if pendingFileCount is stuck nonzero and lastIngestedTimestamp is old, the pipe isn't being triggered at all. Second, query the COPY_HISTORY table function (or INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COPY_HISTORY) scoped to the target table, which shows every file Snowflake actually attempted to load and any per-file error, separate from pipe status.

The two most common root causes: (1) the cloud storage event notification was never correctly wired to the pipe's notification channel — permissions missing, wrong topic/queue referenced, or the notification integration object pointing at the wrong resource — so Snowflake is never actually told new files exist, even though auto_ingest=true is set; this shows up as PENDING_FILE_COUNT staying nonzero with nothing being pulled. (2) files are failing to load due to malformed JSON or a schema mismatch, and with a lenient ON_ERROR setting they fail silently per-file without alerting anyone — this shows up in COPY_HISTORY with a non-SUCCESS status per file, while PIPE_STATUS might look otherwise fine. A third gotcha worth mentioning: auto-ingest only reacts to NEW events going forward from when the pipe/notification was wired up — files that already existed in the stage before that point need a manual ALTER PIPE ... REFRESH to be picked up.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd check is SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS on the pipe — that tells me if it's even being triggered: is pendingFileCount stuck, when did it last actually ingest something. If that looks dead, the problem is almost always that the cloud storage event notification isn't actually reaching Snowflake — a permissions issue or a misconfigured notification integration — even though AUTO_INGEST=TRUE is set on the pipe.

If pipe status looks healthy but rows still aren't there, I'd go straight to COPY_HISTORY for the table, which shows every file Snowflake tried to load and the per-file result. That's usually where I find the second common cause — files are landing and being picked up, but failing to parse because of a schema mismatch or malformed JSON, and with a loose ON_ERROR setting those failures don't surface anywhere unless you go looking in COPY_HISTORY specifically. And if this is a backfill situation where files existed before the pipe was wired up, I'd remember auto-ingest doesn't retroactively pick those up — that needs an explicit ALTER PIPE ... REFRESH.
questions.example:
CREATE PIPE raw_events_pipe
  AUTO_INGEST = TRUE
AS
  COPY INTO raw_events
  FROM @raw_events_stage
  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON)
  ON_ERROR = CONTINUE;

-- Diagnosis
SELECT SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS('raw_events_pipe');

SELECT *
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COPY_HISTORY(
  TABLE_NAME => 'raw_events',
  START_TIME => DATEADD(hours, -24, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
))
WHERE STATUS != 'LOADED';

Only checking SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS and never checking COPY_HISTORY, missing silent per-file load failures
Using ON_ERROR = CONTINUE without any process that reviews COPY_HISTORY for failed files, so bad files vanish silently
Expecting auto-ingest to retroactively pick up files that already existed in the stage before setup
Forgetting the pipe needs its own set of privileges (e.g. on the stage and notification integration) separate from the warehouse running COPY INTO manually

SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS shows whether the pipe is being triggered at all (pendingFileCount, lastIngestedTimestamp)
COPY_HISTORY shows per-file load attempts and errors, independent of pipe status
Most common causes: broken/misconfigured event notification, or silently failing files under a lenient ON_ERROR
Pre-existing files before setup need a manual ALTER PIPE ... REFRESH; auto-ingest only reacts going forward

questions.title: Fixing a SQL-Injectable Dynamic Search Procedure
questions.prompt: A teammate wrote the stored procedure below to let a reporting UI search products by color with a user-selectable sort column. Identify every injection vector in it, then rewrite it safely. Explain specifically why the color value and the sort column name have to be handled differently -- one can be parameterized directly, the other cannot.
questions.modelAnswer:
There are two separate injection vectors here, and they need two different fixes.

The first is @Color: it's concatenated directly into the string inside quotes, so a value like `Red'; DROP TABLE Production.Product; --` gets executed as part of the statement. This is the classic case sp_executesql exists to solve -- @Color is a data value, so it belongs in sp_executesql's parameter list, where SQL Server treats it strictly as data and never as executable text, no matter what characters it contains.

The second is @SortColumn, and it's actually the more dangerous one because it can't be fixed the same way. sp_executesql's parameters only substitute values -- they cannot substitute an identifier like a column name, because `ORDER BY @Param` isn't valid T-SQL (SQL Server would try to sort by a constant, not by a column). That means @SortColumn has to be handled by validation, not parameterization: either whitelist it against a known, fixed list of legal column names before it ever reaches the dynamic string, or at minimum wrap it in QUOTENAME() to neutralize bracket-based injection tricks -- and I'd do both, since QUOTENAME alone doesn't stop someone passing a syntactically valid but unintended column name.

The corrected version below parameterizes @Color through sp_executesql and validates @SortColumn against an explicit allow-list before concatenating it (safely, as an identifier, not a value).
questions.professionalAnswer:
Looking at this procedure, I'd flag it immediately in a code review -- it's building the entire WHERE and ORDER BY clause by gluing strings together, and that's a textbook SQL injection hole. There are actually two different problems stacked on top of each other, and I'd want to be clear they need different fixes. The Color value is a data value, so the right move is sp_executesql with a proper parameter -- that's the whole reason sp_executesql exists, it treats whatever gets passed in purely as data, so even something like a stray apostrophe or an embedded DROP TABLE just becomes a literal string being compared, not code getting executed.

The sort column is trickier, and I'd explain why it can't get the same treatment: you physically cannot parameterize an identifier the way you parameterize a value -- ORDER BY @SomeParam just doesn't do what you'd want, it won't sort by a column, it'll try to sort by whatever that one value is. So for something like a sort column, I always reach for a whitelist -- check the incoming value against the small, fixed list of columns we actually allow sorting by, fall back to a safe default if it's not on the list, and only then build it into the dynamic SQL as an identifier, wrapped in QUOTENAME for good measure.
commonMistakes: Parameterizing only the value and missing that the sort column is a second, separate injection vector
Trying to pass the sort column as an sp_executesql parameter, which doesn't work for identifiers
Relying on QUOTENAME alone for the sort column without an allow-list behind it
Using EXEC() with concatenated strings instead of sp_executesql
Assuming input validation on the UI side is sufficient and skipping server-side protection
keyPoints: sp_executesql parameterizes data values safely; EXEC() with concatenation does not
Identifiers (column/table names) cannot be parameterized -- only values can
Dynamic identifiers must be validated against a whitelist, optionally plus QUOTENAME
Reach for dynamic SQL only when a real identifier or structural element must vary at runtime
SQL injection risk exists even inside stored procedures, not just at the application layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both injection vectors (value and identifier)
Explains why sp_executesql parameters can't substitute identifiers
Provides a correct, safe rewrite using sp_executesql
Includes identifier whitelisting/QUOTENAME for the sort column
Clear overall explanation of the fix

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recurring Deadlock Between Two Order-Processing Procedures
questions.prompt: Two stored procedures are both involved in order processing: usp_UpdateOrderStatus updates the Orders table first, then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount updates OrderDetails first, then Orders. Under heavy load during a sale event, both start failing intermittently with error 1205. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a genuine deadlock rather than ordinary blocking, what SQL Server already did automatically before you even got paged, how you'd capture the diagnostic evidence, and how you'd redesign the two procedures so this stops recurring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Error 1205 is the giveaway on its own -- it's SQL Server's specific "transaction was deadlocked" error, distinct from ordinary blocking (which doesn't raise an error at all; it just makes the waiting session sit there until the lock is released or the query times out). So the first confirmation is simply that message text and code, not a guess.

Before anyone got paged, SQL Server's lock monitor already detected the cycle automatically and picked one of the two transactions as the deadlock victim, rolling it back on its own and raising 1205 in that session, while letting the other transaction proceed normally. That's expected, automatic behavior -- the problem isn't that SQL Server handled a deadlock; it's that the application design is creating deadlocks in the first place.

To get real evidence instead of guessing, I'd capture the actual deadlock graph: either the system_health Extended Events session (which captures deadlock graphs by default on every modern SQL Server instance with zero setup), or trace flag 1222 writing deadlock graphs to the error log, or a live SQL Server Profiler trace with the Deadlock graph event if I need to reproduce it under controlled load. The graph shows exactly which two sessions were involved, which resources (specific rows/keys/pages) each one held and was waiting on, and which queries were running -- that's what turns "it deadlocks sometimes" into "usp_UpdateOrderStatus held a lock on Orders row X while waiting on OrderDetails row Y, and usp_ApplyDiscount had the exact opposite."

The root cause here is visible just from the procedure descriptions, independent of the graph: the two procedures touch the same two tables in opposite order. usp_UpdateOrderStatus locks Orders then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount locks OrderDetails then Orders. Under enough concurrent load, it's inevitable that one session grabs the first lock each procedure needs right as the other grabs the second, and neither can proceed. The fix is to enforce a single, consistent access order across every procedure that touches both tables -- rewrite usp_ApplyDiscount to update Orders before OrderDetails, matching usp_UpdateOrderStatus. I'd also shorten both transactions to only what genuinely needs to be atomic, consider whether the default isolation level is adding unnecessary lock duration for this workload, and add application-side retry logic that catches 1205 specifically and retries the transaction once, since even with consistent ordering, some contention under extreme load is still possible.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point to is that error 1205 is specific -- it's SQL Server's deadlock error, not generic blocking, so I already know what category of problem this is before I even look at the code. And something people sometimes miss: by the time I'm looking at this, SQL Server has already handled the immediate crisis on its own -- it detected the cycle, picked a victim, rolled that one transaction back, and let the other one finish. So I'm not firefighting an active deadlock; I'm investigating why this keeps happening.

To get real evidence I'd go straight to the deadlock graph -- these days that's usually just querying the system_health Extended Events session, since it captures deadlock graphs automatically without me having to turn anything on ahead of time. If I needed something more targeted I'd reach for trace flag 1222 or a Profiler trace with the deadlock graph event. That graph tells me exactly which resources each session was holding and waiting on, which is the proof, not just a theory.

But honestly, in this specific case, I could probably guess the root cause just from the procedure descriptions: one updates Orders then OrderDetails, the other does it backwards. That's the single most common cause of a deadlock -- two pieces of code locking the same two tables in opposite order. My fix is to make every procedure that touches both tables agree on one consistent order, keep the transactions as short as possible so the window for collision is small, and add retry logic around 1205 specifically on the application side as a safety net, since consistent ordering reduces deadlocks dramatically but doesn't mathematically guarantee zero under extreme concurrency.
commonMistakes: Treating ordinary blocking and a deadlock (error 1205) as the same thing
Assuming a deadlock means SQL Server malfunctioned rather than handled an application design flaw
Guessing at the cause instead of capturing the actual deadlock graph
Fixing only the symptom (retrying) without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Wrapping the entire procedure in one long transaction instead of minimizing what's actually atomic
keyPoints: Error 1205 specifically identifies a deadlock, distinct from ordinary blocking
SQL Server automatically detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen victim
system_health Extended Events / trace flag 1222 / Profiler capture the deadlock graph for real evidence
Root cause here is inconsistent table access order across the two procedures
Fix: enforce consistent access order, keep transactions short, add retry logic for 1205

questions.title: A Nightly Staging Query's Runtime Quietly Tripled
questions.prompt: A nightly ETL step that filters Sales.SalesOrderHeader by a date range used to finish in under a minute. After a recent, unrelated application release, it now takes over 20 minutes most nights, even though nobody touched the query text itself. Walk through your full diagnostic process, in the order you'd actually do it, to find the real cause and prove your fix worked.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd work outward from the query itself before looking anywhere else, because the fact that nobody touched this query's text doesn't mean nothing that affects it changed.

First, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run it, looking specifically for whether an operation that used to be an Index Seek is now a Scan -- that's the single most common visible signature of a regressed query. I'd also compare estimated vs. actual row counts on each operator; a big gap there points at stale statistics giving the optimizer bad cardinality estimates, which can push it toward a much worse plan even though the query text is identical.

Second, I'd capture SET STATISTICS TIME and SET STATISTICS IO output and compare it mentally against what I'd expect for this table's size. If CPU time and elapsed time are close, it's genuinely doing more logical work; if elapsed time is much higher than CPU time, something else -- blocking, waits, disk I/O contention -- is adding wait time on top of comparable actual work, and I'd pivot to sys.dm_exec_requests / sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks to see what wait type is dominating.

Third, I'd specifically check whether the query's WHERE clause is still SARGable the way it was before. The "unrelated application release" detail is a flag: if the application layer changed how it passes the date parameter -- say, switching from a DATETIME parameter to a string that now gets implicitly converted, or wrapping the column in a function somewhere upstream that got introduced in the release -- that alone can silently turn a seek into a scan without anyone touching this specific query's text.

Fourth, if this runs as a parameterized query or inside a stored procedure, I'd consider parameter sniffing: if the release changed what date ranges get passed first after a recompile, SQL Server may have cached a plan optimized for a very different-sized result set than what's typically requested now. I'd check sys.dm_exec_query_stats for that procedure's cached plan and compare it against a fresh OPTION (RECOMPILE) run.

Fifth, I'd check whether an index this query relied on was changed, disabled, or had its fill factor/maintenance schedule altered as part of the release, and whether statistics were updated recently -- a large data load with no corresponding stats update is a very common, very quiet cause of exactly this symptom.

Finally, I'd correlate the actual onset against the release timeline and any index maintenance job history, form a specific hypothesis from whichever of the above turned up concrete evidence, apply the fix (rebuild/update statistics, restore a missing index, fix an implicit conversion, add OPTION (RECOMPILE) or a plan guide for parameter sniffing), and then prove it with a direct before/after comparison of logical reads via SET STATISTICS IO -- that number is the most reliable proof a fix genuinely reduced work, independent of how busy the server happened to be at the moment I measured it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't jump straight to 'rebuild the index' or 'update stats' -- I'd want to actually see what changed first. So step one for me is always the actual execution plan, Ctrl+M, run the query, and look specifically for a scan where I'd expect a seek, plus a big gap between estimated and actual row counts, because that gap is basically SQL Server telling you its statistics are lying to it.

Step two, I'd pull SET STATISTICS TIME and IO and look at whether CPU time and elapsed time line up. If they're close, the engine's genuinely doing more work. If elapsed time is way bigger than CPU time, I know to go look at waits and blocking instead of the query logic itself.

The detail that really jumps out at me in this scenario is 'an unrelated application release' right before this started. That's exactly the kind of thing that quietly breaks SARGability without anyone touching the SQL -- maybe the app now sends the date as a string instead of a proper date, and now there's an implicit conversion happening on every row. I'd check that specifically.

If this lives inside a stored procedure, parameter sniffing is next on my list -- the first execution after a recompile caches a plan shaped for whatever parameter came in that first time, and if the typical date range changed after the release, that cached plan might be wrong for almost every call since. And I'd double check whether an index got dropped, disabled, or just went stale from a big data load with no corresponding stats update around the same time as the release.

Whatever I land on, I don't call it fixed until I've got a before-and-after comparison of logical reads from STATISTICS IO -- that number doesn't lie the way timing can when the server's under different load each time I test.

Jumping to 'rebuild all the indexes' without first checking the actual plan for a scan-vs-seek regression
Ignoring that an unrelated application change can break SARGability through implicit conversion
Not checking for parameter sniffing on parameterized/stored-procedure queries
Declaring victory based on a single wall-clock timing instead of logical reads before/after
keyPoints: Start with the actual execution plan: look for scan-vs-seek regressions and estimated/actual row count gaps
SET STATISTICS TIME/IO separates CPU-bound work from waiting/blocking
An unrelated release can break SARGability via implicit conversion or a changed parameter type
Parameter sniffing is a real suspect for parameterized/stored-procedure queries after a recompile
Check for dropped/disabled indexes and stale statistics correlated with the release timeline
Prove the fix with a before/after logical-reads comparison, not just a timing

questions.title: Diagnosing Unexpected Totals From CALCULATE Inside SUMX
questions.prompt: A measure written as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), FILTER(Customer, [Customer Measure] > 100)), where [Customer Measure] itself calls CALCULATE on Sales, returns totals that shift unexpectedly when a product-category slicer is applied - numbers that don't match a hand-calculated expectation. Walk through how you'd diagnose the context-transition behavior causing this.
questions.modelAnswer: The core thing to check is what happens to [Customer Measure] inside that FILTER. FILTER(Customer, ...) iterates the Customer table row by row - that's row context. [Customer Measure] is a measure reference, and every measure reference is implicitly wrapped in its own CALCULATE, which means context transition fires for every single customer row: the current customer's row context gets converted into a one-customer filter context before [Customer Measure] evaluates. Critically, that implicit CALCULATE also inherits whatever filter context is already active outside, including the product-category slicer. So [Customer Measure] isn't being evaluated against 'this customer, all products' per row; it's being evaluated against 'this customer, intersected with whatever category the slicer currently has selected.' That's almost certainly the source of the shifting numbers: as the slicer changes, the per-row result of [Customer Measure] changes for every customer, which changes which customers pass the >100 threshold inside FILTER, which changes the set of customers the outer SUM runs against - a compounding effect, not a simple scaling. To diagnose concretely: temporarily rewrite [Customer Measure] as a plain CALCULATE expression inline so the context transition is visible instead of hidden behind a measure reference; use a VAR to capture [Customer Measure]'s value for one specific, known customer under two different slicer selections and compare them directly - if they differ, that confirms the slicer is reaching into the per-row evaluation via context transition, which is expected behavior, not a bug; then decide whether that's actually wanted - if the threshold should be evaluated against each customer's all-time total regardless of the slicer, wrap the inner measure's CALCULATE with ALL(Product) or REMOVEFILTERS(Product) to deliberately cut it off from the slicer, rather than letting it inherit by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd zero in on is that FILTER(Customer, [Customer Measure] > 100) is evaluating [Customer Measure] once per customer row, and since that's a measure reference sitting inside row context, it's implicitly wrapped in its own CALCULATE - so context transition fires for every row, and that implicit CALCULATE picks up whatever filter context is already active, including the category slicer. So the per-customer threshold check isn't really 'does this customer's all-time value exceed 100,' it's 'does this customer's value under the currently selected category exceed 100' - and that set of qualifying customers shifts every time the slicer changes, which compounds into the outer SUM. To prove that's what's happening, I'd isolate one known customer with a VAR, evaluate [Customer Measure] for them under two different slicer states, and compare the numbers directly - if they differ, that confirms the slicer is reaching inside the per-row evaluation. Then it's a design decision: if the threshold is supposed to ignore the slicer, I'd wrap the inner measure's CALCULATE with ALL or REMOVEFILTERS on the category column so it stops inheriting that context.
questions.example: Debug step: VAR TestCustomerValue = CALCULATE([Customer Measure], Customer[CustomerKey] = 123) RETURN TestCustomerValue - evaluated once with the category slicer set to 'Bikes' and once cleared, to see directly whether the per-customer value is slicer-dependent.

Not realizing context transition means the implicit CALCULATE inherits the active filter context, including slicers
Treating the shifting totals as a bug instead of correct (if unintended) behavior that needs a deliberate ALL/REMOVEFILTERS fix
Debugging by staring at the final number instead of isolating one row's value with a VAR
keyPoints: Measure references inside row context trigger implicit CALCULATE / context transition
Context transition inherits the currently active filter context, including slicers, unless explicitly overridden
FILTER iterating a table creates row context for every measure called inside it
Isolate one row's value with VAR under different filter states to confirm the behavior
Use ALL/REMOVEFILTERS inside the inner measure if the threshold should ignore the slicer

questions.title: A Percent-of-Total Measure Ignores the Slicer
questions.prompt: A '% of Total' measure was built as DIVIDE([Sales], CALCULATE([Sales], ALL(Sales))). Stakeholders report that when they select a single region in a slicer, the percentages across the visible categories don't sum to 100% - they're much smaller than expected. Diagnose the cause and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: This is working exactly as ALL is defined to work - the symptom isn't a bug, it's a mismatch between what the measure computes and what the stakeholders actually want. ALL(Sales) clears every filter on Sales unconditionally, including the region slicer, so the denominator is always the worldwide total across every region, every time, no matter what's selected. When a user filters to one region, the numerator shrinks to that region's sales but the denominator stays at the full worldwide total - so the percentages correctly reflect 'this category's share of everyone, everywhere,' which only sums to 100% when nothing is filtered, and sums to something much smaller once a region is selected, exactly as reported. What the stakeholders actually want is a visual total: a percentage of what's currently selected, the one region, not of the whole dataset. That's ALLSELECTED's job specifically - it keeps the filters applied outside the visual, the region slicer, and only clears the breakdown generated by the visual itself. Swapping ALL(Sales) for ALLSELECTED() in the denominator fixes it: the denominator becomes 'total sales for the currently selected region,' which the numerators, each category's sales within that region, correctly sum to 100% of.
questions.professionalAnswer: This isn't actually broken DAX, it's answering a different question than the one being asked. ALL(Sales) wipes out every filter on that table, the region slicer included, so no matter what someone picks, the denominator is always the full worldwide total. That's why, once you filter to one region, the numbers only add up to that region's small slice of the world instead of 100% - the math is doing exactly what ALL tells it to do. What the stakeholders actually want is for the denominator to respect their region selection and only ignore the category breakdown the visual itself creates - that's precisely what ALLSELECTED does. Swapping ALL(Sales) for ALLSELECTED() in the denominator means the total becomes 'everything selected, in this case the one region,' and the category percentages go back to summing to 100% of that.
questions.example: Before the fix, selecting 'West' region: numerator = West's category sales, denominator = worldwide total, so percentages sum to roughly West's share of the world, well under 100%. After the fix: denominator = West's total, so percentages correctly sum to 100% of West.

Trying to 'fix' it by adding more filter arguments to ALL instead of switching to ALLSELECTED
Not testing the measure with a slicer selection active before shipping it, so the discrepancy wasn't caught earlier
Assuming ALLSELECTED and ALL are interchangeable because they both start with 'ALL'
keyPoints: ALL clears report-level/slicer filters too, not just the visual's own breakdown
A percentage that should respect slicer selections needs ALLSELECTED, not ALL
Always test ratio/percent-of-total measures with a slicer active, not just unfiltered
The underlying DAX wasn't broken - it was answering a different question than the one asked

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses ALL as clearing the slicer filter too
Explains why percentages don't sum to 100% once filtered

questions.title: A Nightly Procedure That Used to Finish in Minutes Now Takes Hours
questions.prompt: A nightly stored procedure that updates loyalty points for every customer who made a purchase that day used to finish in under five minutes. Over the last two months it's crept up to three hours, and nobody changed the procedure's code. When you open it, you find it's built around a cursor that loops through qualifying customers one at a time, calling an UPDATE inside the loop. Walk through how you'd confirm the cursor is the real problem, why its cost grows disproportionately as the table grows, and how you'd rewrite it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't assume the cursor is guilty just because cursors have a bad reputation -- I'd confirm it with SET STATISTICS TIME and IO around the existing procedure, and separately time a rewritten set-based version against the same day's data, so the comparison is based on actual numbers rather than instinct. I'd also check whether the cursor's own underlying SELECT has degraded (stale statistics causing a scan instead of a seek on the qualifying-customers query), since that's a second, compounding problem that's easy to miss if you only blame the loop itself.

The reason a cursor's cost grows disproportionately as a table grows isn't just that there are more rows to loop over -- it's that every iteration carries fixed per-row overhead (a context switch between the engine and the cursor machinery, its own mini-transaction and log record for each UPDATE, lock acquisition and release every single time) that a single set-based statement pays only once, not once per row. As the qualifying-customer count has grown month over month with the business, that per-row overhead has been multiplying against a growing row count, which is exactly the kind of cost curve that looks fine for a long time and then visibly takes off -- nobody changed the code, but the data volume the same code runs against did.

The rewrite replaces the entire loop with a single set-based UPDATE ... FROM that joins the same filtering logic the cursor used to decide which customers qualify, letting the engine process the whole batch as one operation instead of thousands of tiny ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually prove it's the cursor rather than just assuming it, because cursors get blamed a lot but I want real numbers. I'd run STATISTICS TIME and IO on the existing procedure, and time a rewritten set-based version against the same data, and compare. I'd also take a look at the cursor's own underlying query, because sometimes the real second problem is that it's degraded from a seek to a scan as the table's grown, on top of the cursor overhead itself. As for why this crept up without the code changing -- a cursor pays a fixed cost per row, every iteration, things like its own mini-transaction and locking overhead, and a single set-based statement only pays that cost once for the whole batch. As the number of qualifying customers has grown with the business over the last couple months, that per-row cost has been compounding against a bigger row count every single night, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine for a long time and then suddenly doesn't. The actual fix is just replacing the whole loop with one UPDATE statement that joins against the same qualifying criteria the cursor used, so the engine handles it as a single batch operation instead of thousands of small ones.

Not profiling with STATISTICS TIME/IO before concluding the cursor is the bottleneck
Rewriting to a WHILE loop over a temp table instead of a true single set-based statement, which is still slow
Not checking whether the cursor's underlying SELECT has also degraded due to stale statistics

questions.title: Blocking Caused by a Missing Index, Not a Bug in the Code
questions.prompt: Every weekday around 10 AM, the order-entry application starts timing out for a few minutes. SQL Server's Activity Monitor shows dozens of INSERT statements from the app blocked behind a single SELECT from a management report that joins Orders to OrderLines. The report query and the INSERT statements haven't changed in months. sys.dm_tran_locks shows the report query holding a table-level (not row-level) lock on OrderLines. Diagnose why a plain SELECT is blocking INSERTs this badly, and fix it.
questions.code:
SELECT o.OrderId, ol.ProductId, ol.Quantity
FROM Orders o
JOIN OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderId = o.OrderId
WHERE o.SalesRepId = @RepId;
questions.modelAnswer:
A SELECT without an explicit hint doesn't normally take a table lock, so the first question is how that scan turned into one. With no supporting index on OrderLines for whatever predicate or join path the optimizer chose, the engine has to touch a large number of rows via a scan, taking a shared lock on each one it visits. SQL Server has a finite lock memory budget, and when the number of individual locks held by one statement crosses an internal threshold, it automatically escalates from many fine-grained row/page locks to a single table-level lock to reduce lock management overhead. That table-level shared lock is compatible with other readers but blocks writers outright, which is exactly why INSERTs into OrderLines pile up behind it even though the report is 'just reading.'

The fix starts with the execution plan: confirm there's a scan (not a seek) on OrderLines and identify which column the join or filter actually needs. If OrderLines has no index on OrderId (or on whatever column anchors the join to Orders), add a nonclustered index on that column, with included columns for ProductId and Quantity if this query is frequent enough to want a fully covering index. A seek against that index touches far fewer rows, likely staying well under the escalation threshold. If the table is simply very large and even a seek'ed range returns many rows, enabling Read Committed Snapshot Isolation removes the shared-lock-vs-insert conflict entirely for this pattern, since readers would work off row versions rather than blocking locks - though that's an instance-wide (or database-wide) behavior change that needs sign-off, not a drive-by fix. I'd pair the index fix with monitoring for LOCK_ESCALATION events going forward so this class of problem surfaces before users notice it again.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by not trusting 'nothing changed in the code' as proof nothing changed - data volume grows even when queries don't, and a join that used to be cheap can quietly cross the row-count threshold where the optimizer stops seeking and starts scanning. So first I pull the actual execution plan for that report query and check OrderLines for a scan versus a seek. If it's scanning, that tells me there's no supporting index for the join, and all those row locks it's picking up along the way are what's triggering SQL Server's automatic lock escalation to a table lock - which is the real reason a read is blocking writes so hard. My fix is almost always to add the missing index first, because a seek that only touches the rows it needs rarely escalates at all. If I add the index and it's still escalating because the table's genuinely huge and the result set is wide, then I'd bring RCSI into the conversation as a bigger architectural change, but I wouldn't reach for that first since it changes isolation behavior for everyone, not just this one report.
questions.example:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_OrderLines_OrderId ON dbo.OrderLines (OrderId) INCLUDE (ProductId, Quantity);
-- Verify with: SET STATISTICS IO ON; and re-check the plan for an Index Seek instead of a Clustered Index Scan on OrderLines.
commonMistakes: Assuming a SELECT can't cause serious blocking, so looking everywhere except the report query itself
Jumping straight to NOLOCK hints or snapshot isolation without first checking whether a missing index is the real root cause
Not checking sys.dm_tran_locks or the execution plan to confirm an escalation actually happened versus assuming it from symptoms alone
Adding an index without included columns, fixing the seek but still causing extra key lookups under load
Treating the fix as done without monitoring for future LOCK_ESCALATION events as data grows
keyPoints: Lock escalation automatically converts many row/page locks into one table lock once a statement exceeds the lock count threshold
A missing index forcing a scan is the most common trigger for escalation on an otherwise 'simple' read
Confirm with the execution plan (scan vs seek) and sys.dm_tran_locks before proposing a fix
A targeted covering index is usually the right first fix; RCSI is a bigger, instance-level decision
Index design should include the columns actually returned, not just the join key, to avoid extra lookups

Identifies missing index as the likely root cause and how to confirm it
Proposes a correct, appropriately scoped index fix
