questions.title: A Margin Measure That's Right on Every Row but 'Wrong' on the Grand Total
questions.prompt: A Profit Margin % measure is defined as DIVIDE([Total Profit],[Total Sales]) and shows correct, verified percentages on every product row of a table visual. Finance insists the Grand Total row is wrong, because it doesn't match what you'd get by averaging the visible row percentages. Explain what's actually happening and how you'd resolve the disagreement with Finance.
questions.code:
Profit Margin % = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])
Total Profit = SUM(Sales[Profit])
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount])
questions.modelAnswer:
The behavior Finance is flagging isn't a bug in the measure - it's expected, correct behavior for a ratio that isn't additive across the grain of the visual. At the Grand Total row, DAX re-evaluates DIVIDE([Total Profit],[Total Sales]) in the filter context of the total, which means it sums profit across all products, sums sales across all products, and divides those two aggregated totals. That is mathematically the weighted average margin across the business, weighted by each product's sales volume. A simple arithmetic average of the per-row percentages, by contrast, would give every product equal weight regardless of how much it actually sold, which is a different (and usually less meaningful) number for a margin KPI. Those two numbers will diverge whenever product-level sales volumes vary significantly, and that's exactly the situation here.

Before telling Finance 'it's working as intended,' I'd still run a sanity check to rule out an actual bug masquerading as this behavior - things like an inactive or bidirectional relationship, a slicer not applying consistently, or a stray ALLSELECTED/ALL somewhere in a related measure that would make the total ignore filters the rows respect. If the raw Total Profit and Total Sales numbers at the grand total tie out to the sum of the visible rows' underlying profit and sales (not their displayed percentages), that confirms the measure is correct and the disagreement is really about which statistic Finance wants to see. At that point I'd explain the weighted-average interpretation directly, and if they genuinely want a simple average of the displayed percentages for some other purpose, I'd build that as an explicitly separate, clearly labeled measure using AVERAGEX over the visible products rather than overwrite the correct weighted margin.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, the first thing I'd do is not panic and assume my DAX is broken, because this exact complaint comes up constantly with any kind of percentage or ratio measure. I'd explain to Finance that the total row isn't averaging the percentages they see - it's recalculating the ratio from the underlying totals, profit over sales, both summed across everything in view. That's actually the weighted average, which gives bigger products more say in the number, and it's usually the more honest number for a margin KPI than treating a tiny product and a huge product as equally important. Before I go explain that, though, I always double check the raw numbers underneath - pull Total Profit and Total Sales at the total level and confirm they really do equal the sum of what's on the rows - because I want to rule out that something like a sneaky bidirectional relationship is actually causing a real discrepancy before I confidently tell Finance 'this is correct.' If after that check it really is just the weighted-vs-simple-average distinction, I'll offer to add a separate, clearly labeled simple-average measure if that's genuinely what they want for some other view, but I wouldn't change the margin measure itself to do something mathematically less correct.
commonMistakes: Assuming the total is wrong just because it doesn't match an average of the displayed row percentages
'Fixing' it by wrapping the measure in AVERAGEX over the ratio, which silently changes the math to something less correct for a margin KPI
Not validating the raw underlying totals before concluding the behavior is expected rather than a real bug
Not recognizing that this is a filter-context re-evaluation, not a context-transition issue, and explaining it with the wrong mechanism
Failing to communicate the distinction to stakeholders in plain terms, leaving them thinking the model itself is unreliable
keyPoints: Ratio measures aren't additive - the total re-evaluates the ratio of aggregated totals, not an average of row ratios
This total represents a sales-weighted average margin, which is usually more meaningful than a simple average
Validate raw totals first to rule out an actual bug (bad relationship, stray ALL/ALLSELECTED) before concluding it's expected behavior
Offer a separate, explicitly labeled measure if stakeholders truly want the simple-average interpretation
Clear communication of 'why' is as important as the technical diagnosis here

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why the total differs from a row-average correctly
Describes concrete validation steps to rule out a real bug
Correctly characterizes the total as a weighted average and why that matters
Proposes an appropriate way to satisfy a genuine alternate requirement without breaking the measure

questions.title: A Pipeline That Fails on Two Nights Out of Seven, With No Retry Policy
questions.prompt: A nightly Data Factory pipeline copies data from an on-premises SQL Server to Azure Data Lake using a self-hosted integration runtime. It fails roughly two nights out of seven with a generic 'ErrorCode=SqlOperationFailed, Code=121, Timeout expired' message. There is no retry policy configured on the Copy activity. A manual rerun the next morning always succeeds. Describe how you'd investigate this and what you'd fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
A generic SQL timeout on an intermittent schedule points me toward resource contention or network conditions rather than a logic bug, since the same pipeline and query succeed cleanly most nights and always on manual rerun. I'd start in the Monitor hub to confirm exactly which activity failed and its duration right up to the timeout, then check the self-hosted integration runtime's node health (CPU, memory, available connections) around the failure window, since a single-node self-hosted IR is a shared resource that can be starved by other on-premises activity - most commonly overlapping backup jobs, index maintenance windows, or other batch processes that happen to run at a similar time but not every night. I'd also check whether the source query itself does a large, unfiltered scan that depends on how much data has accumulated, since a slow night might simply be a night where the extract had more rows to move or the source server was mid-maintenance.

Once I understand the pattern, I'd apply two layers of fix. First, a basic safety net: add a retry policy on the Copy activity with a sensible interval and increase the command timeout, since 'fails twice a week, succeeds on manual rerun' is exactly the signature a modest retry policy is meant to catch automatically instead of requiring someone to notice and intervene by morning. Second, the actual root-cause fix: if it's resource contention from a single self-hosted IR node, I'd look at scaling to a second node for high availability and load distribution, or rescheduling the pipeline to avoid the overlapping on-prem maintenance window entirely. I'd also set up alerting on pipeline failure so this gets caught the same night rather than discovered by a user the next day, and log activity-level metrics to Log Analytics so the next intermittent issue has a historical pattern to compare against immediately.
questions.professionalAnswer: Intermittent plus 'works fine on manual rerun' is basically the classic signature of a resource or environment problem, not a code problem, so I wouldn't spend much time re-reading the pipeline logic itself. I'd go straight to the Monitor hub to nail down exactly which activity and how long it ran before timing out, and then I'd check the self-hosted IR's node health for those specific nights - CPU, memory, whatever else was running on that box around the same time. In my experience it's almost always something else on-prem competing for resources, like a backup window that doesn't run every single night. While I'm there I'd also just add a retry policy on the Copy activity, because honestly there's no excuse for not having one on an unattended nightly job - that alone would probably make this stop being a human-noticed problem even before I find the deeper cause. Longer term, if it really is IR resource contention, I'd push for a second IR node for redundancy and look at shifting the schedule a bit so it's not fighting with whatever else is hogging that server.
commonMistakes: Assuming it's a pipeline logic bug and re-reviewing the Copy activity configuration instead of checking IR and source-server resource health
Not adding a retry policy as a basic safety net, leaving an unattended nightly job with zero resilience to transient failures
Not checking for concurrent on-premises jobs (backups, maintenance) that could explain the intermittent pattern
Treating 'manual rerun works' as proof the problem is solved rather than evidence pointing toward a timing/resource issue
Not considering single self-hosted IR node as a single point of failure/bottleneck
keyPoints: Intermittent failure plus successful manual rerun points to resource contention or timing, not pipeline logic
Check self-hosted IR node health and concurrent on-premises jobs around the failure window
Add a retry policy and increase command timeout as an immediate safety net
Consider scaling the self-hosted IR to multiple nodes for both capacity and high availability
Set up alerting and centralized logging so intermittent issues are caught the same night

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons toward resource/timing contention rather than a code bug
Describes concrete diagnostic steps (Monitor hub, IR node health, concurrent jobs)
Proposes retry policy and timeout tuning as immediate mitigation
Proposes IR scaling/HA or scheduling fix as the deeper remedy
Clarity

questions.title: Dynamic RLS Works in 'View As Roles' but Not for Real Users
questions.prompt: You've configured dynamic Row-Level Security in a Power BI semantic model so regional managers see only their own region, using USERPRINCIPALNAME() looked up against a UserRegion mapping table. Testing with 'View as Roles' in Desktop filters correctly for every region. After publishing, several real regional managers report they can see every region's data once logged into the Service. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
'View as Roles' in Desktop only simulates the DAX filter logic itself - it never exercises the parts of RLS enforcement that only exist in the Service, which is exactly where I'd look first. The single most common cause of 'RLS works in testing but not for real users' is that those specific users hold a workspace role of Admin, Member, or Contributor rather than Viewer (or app access without an elevated workspace role) - RLS is enforced only for Viewer-level access and for apps/shared content, and anyone with edit-level workspace permissions bypasses it entirely by design, since they're expected to be able to see the underlying data to build and maintain content. The second thing I'd check is whether the roles were actually assigned to the affected users or their security groups under the dataset's Security settings in the Service - defining a role in Desktop does nothing in the Service until someone explicitly assigns members to it there, and that assignment step is easy to miss or to apply only to some users during rollout.

If both of those check out, I'd check for case-sensitivity or formatting mismatches between USERPRINCIPALNAME() and the Email column in UserRegionMap - trailing whitespace, differing casing conventions, or an email alias versus UPN mismatch will make LOOKUPVALUE return blank, and depending on how the rest of the model handles a blank region, that can silently resolve to 'no filter applied' rather than an error. Finally, I'd check whether any of the affected users are intentionally or accidentally members of more than one role; Power BI unions (ORs) the filters from every role a user belongs to, so if a user is in both 'Regional - West' and some broader role like 'Global Readonly' that doesn't filter by region at all, they'll see everything, which looks identical to RLS 'not working' but is actually RLS working exactly as configured.
questions.professionalAnswer: Whenever I hear 'it worked in View as Roles but not for real users,' my first question is always about workspace permissions, because that's the gap nobody remembers until they hit it: RLS simply doesn't apply to anyone with Admin, Member, or Contributor access to the workspace - only Viewers and app consumers get filtered. So I'd check what role those specific managers actually have on the workspace before I touch the DAX at all. If they're genuinely Viewers, then I'd go check the Security settings on the published dataset in the Service, because defining roles in Desktop is only half the job - you have to go assign actual users or groups to those roles after publishing, and that step gets skipped surprisingly often during a rollout. After that I'd sanity-check the USERPRINCIPALNAME-to-email matching for case or whitespace issues, and I'd specifically check whether any of these users are sitting in more than one role, since Power BI doesn't intersect multiple roles' filters, it unions them - so being in a second, broader role can silently cancel out the regional restriction even though the regional role itself is configured correctly.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that workspace Admin, Member, and Contributor roles bypass RLS entirely, regardless of role assignment
Assuming defining roles in Desktop automatically applies them in the Service without explicit role assignment under dataset Security
Not checking for case/whitespace mismatches between USERPRINCIPALNAME() and the mapping table's email column
Not recognizing that membership in multiple roles unions (not intersects) the resulting access
Treating 'View as Roles' success in Desktop as proof the Service behavior will be identical
keyPoints: RLS is enforced only for Viewer-level/app access, not for Admin, Member, or Contributor workspace roles
Roles must be explicitly assigned to users or groups under the dataset's Security settings in the Service
USERPRINCIPALNAME() matching issues (case, whitespace, alias vs UPN) can silently produce no filter
Multiple role membership unions permissions rather than intersecting them
Desktop's 'View as Roles' doesn't exercise Service-only enforcement gaps

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies workspace-role bypass as the primary likely cause
Identifies missing role assignment in Service Security settings
Explains multi-role union behavior correctly
Mentions USERPRINCIPALNAME matching issues as a secondary check
Clarity

questions.title: A Scheduled Refresh That Only Times Out on Monday Mornings
questions.prompt: A Power BI semantic model refreshes through an on-premises data gateway against a SQL Server source. The scheduled refresh succeeds every day except Monday mornings, when it reliably fails with a gateway timeout. Manually triggering the refresh an hour later always works. What's your diagnostic process, and what's the likely explanation?
questions.modelAnswer:
A failure pattern that's specific to the first refresh after the weekend points me toward something that happens on weekends and is usually finished by the time someone manually retries an hour later. I'd pull the gateway logs (via the on-premises data gateway app, or the admin center's gateway diagnostics) around the exact failure time to confirm it's genuinely a timeout and not something else masquerading as one, and then I'd ask the DBA or infrastructure team what runs against that SQL Server over the weekend - full backups, index rebuild/reorg maintenance jobs, or a weekly batch catch-up are all common candidates that can still be running early Monday morning and competing hard for I/O and CPU on the source server, or in some cases still holding locks that make the refresh's queries wait. I'd also check whether the gateway machine itself goes through a weekend patch/restart cycle that leaves it under-resourced or still warming up right when the Monday refresh kicks off.

Once I've correlated the failure window against whatever weekend job is actually running, the fix usually has two parts. The immediate mitigation is to shift the Monday refresh time later, past the point where the weekend job reliably finishes, and to add a retry policy with a reasonable delay so a near-miss doesn't require manual intervention. The deeper fix, if this gateway is a single point of failure, is to set up a gateway cluster with two or more members for both resilience and load distribution, and to coordinate directly with whoever owns the weekend maintenance job so its completion time is known and the refresh schedule is deliberately set after it, rather than guessing at a safe gap.
questions.professionalAnswer: A failure that only ever shows up on Monday mornings is basically begging me to look at what happens over the weekend, so that's where I'd go first rather than second-guessing the refresh configuration itself. I'd check the gateway logs right around the failure time to confirm it's a real timeout, and then go ask whoever owns that SQL Server what's running Saturday and Sunday - backups, index maintenance, weekly catch-up jobs - because it's extremely common for one of those to still be running or to have just finished in a way that leaves the server resource-starved right when the scheduled refresh kicks off. The fact that a manual retry an hour later always works is a big clue too - it tells me whatever's contending for resources has usually cleared by then. My fix would be twofold: push the scheduled refresh time later so it's safely past that weekend job's typical finish time, and add a retry policy so a near-miss doesn't need someone to notice and manually rerun it. If the gateway itself turns out to be a single machine with no redundancy, I'd also push to get it clustered, since relying on one box for something this business-critical is its own risk independent of the Monday timing issue.
commonMistakes: Assuming the gateway itself is unreliable without checking logs or correlating with other scheduled jobs
Not investigating what runs on the source server over the weekend before proposing a fix
Simply increasing the timeout without investigating the underlying resource contention
Not considering a single gateway as a point of failure/bottleneck needing a cluster
Not coordinating with the team that owns the weekend maintenance job
keyPoints: Correlate the Monday-only failure pattern with weekend batch/maintenance jobs on the source server
Use gateway logs and admin center diagnostics to confirm the failure is genuinely a timeout
Shifting the refresh schedule later and adding retry policy is the immediate mitigation
A gateway cluster addresses both resilience and resource contention long-term
Cross-team coordination with the source system's maintenance owners is part of the real fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons toward weekend-job correlation as the diagnostic approach
Describes concrete diagnostic steps (logs, admin center, correlation)
Proposes scheduling/retry mitigation
Proposes gateway HA/clustering as the deeper fix

questions.title: Diagnosing Duplicate Rows After Backfilling an Incremental dbt Model
questions.prompt: A dbt model using incremental_strategy='append' (not merge) has been running nightly for months. You just ran a one-off backfill to reprocess the last 10 days after an upstream bug fix, using a normal incremental run (not --full-refresh). Now downstream reports are showing roughly double the row counts for that window. Diagnose what happened and how you'd fix both the immediate data and the model going forward.
questions.modelAnswer:
The append strategy has no unique_key and no update/delete semantics -- it's a pure INSERT of whatever rows the model's SELECT returns for that run, and it was never designed to be idempotent against reprocessing. Running a normal incremental run over the same 10-day window a second time, after that data was already loaded the first time, just inserts the same rows again on top of what's already there, because append never checks whether a row already exists downstream. That's exactly why the window shows roughly double row counts and nowhere else does.

The immediate fix is to remove the duplicated window's rows -- identify them by run timestamp, a staged snapshot, or the known date range, delete them, and reload once -- or, if the model's logic is deterministic and reprocessing the full history is affordable, run a single --full-refresh instead.

Going forward, switch the model to incremental_strategy='merge' with an appropriate unique_key (a natural key, or a surrogate key built on business key plus date), which makes reprocessing and backfills idempotent -- rerunning the same window updates existing rows rather than duplicating them. Also add a uniqueness test (e.g. dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns) so this class of issue gets caught immediately next time, and document that backfills on append-strategy models require a manual dedup step or a full-refresh until the strategy is changed.
questions.professionalAnswer:
What happened is pretty mechanical once you know append doesn't have a unique_key: it just inserts whatever the SELECT returns, with zero awareness of whether those rows are already in the table. Rerunning a normal incremental run over a window that was already loaded just stacks a second copy of everything on top -- hence the window doubling and nowhere else.

For the immediate fix, I'd isolate and remove the duplicated rows for that 10-day window and reload once, or just full-refresh the whole model if that's cheap enough and the logic is deterministic. For the real fix, I'd switch the model to merge with a real unique_key, because that's what actually makes backfills safe -- rerun the same window as many times as you want and it just updates in place instead of stacking duplicates. I'd also add a uniqueness test on the model so if this ever happens again, it fails loudly in CI instead of someone noticing doubled numbers in a downstream report days later.
commonMistakes: Assuming any incremental strategy is automatically idempotent on rerun
Using append for a model that will ever need ad hoc backfills or reprocessing
Not having a uniqueness test that would have caught the duplication immediately
Defaulting to --full-refresh as the fix without addressing the strategy mismatch that caused it
Not communicating the data quality incident to downstream consumers before silently patching it
keyPoints: append has no unique_key/upsert logic, so reprocessing duplicates rows
merge with unique_key is idempotent for backfills and reruns
Immediate fix requires deduping the affected window or a controlled full-refresh
Add a uniqueness test to catch recurrence
Document the backfill procedure appropriate to the model's incremental strategy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses append's lack of idempotency as the root cause
Proposes a correct immediate remediation
Proposes the correct long-term fix (merge + unique_key)
Mentions a test/detection improvement
Clear overall explanation

questions.title: An Airflow SLA Miss Alert Never Fired for a Pipeline That Was Actually Late
questions.prompt: A critical nightly DAG that feeds an executive dashboard finished 90 minutes late last night, but no SLA miss alert was sent -- the on-call analytics engineer only found out when a VP asked why the dashboard was stale. The DAG has sla=timedelta(hours=1) set on the final task and an sla_miss_callback configured. Diagnose the likely causes and what you'd check first.
questions.modelAnswer:
Airflow's SLA check is evaluated by the scheduler on a periodic loop, not actively triggered by the task itself -- so the first thing to check is whether the scheduler was healthy and actually running its SLA-checking cycle during that window; a backlogged, restarted, or overloaded scheduler can simply miss the check.

Second, and the most common root cause in practice: the sla_miss_callback itself may have raised an exception and failed silently. A broken callback -- a bad Slack webhook URL, an expired credential, a typo in the notification code -- throws when Airflow tries to invoke it, and that failure to alert is itself not surfaced prominently anywhere except the scheduler logs, so the team never sees it. Checking the scheduler logs for that exact window, specifically for errors during SLA callback execution, is the single highest-value next step.

Also worth checking: that the SLA was actually attached to the correct task and that the DAG wasn't paused or affected by catchup in a way that changed when runs were being evaluated. The deeper fix, regardless of which specific cause is found, is adding an independent freshness check on the dashboard's underlying data that doesn't depend on Airflow's SLA mechanism at all -- relying on a single alerting path for something executive-facing is itself the real problem being exposed here.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is scheduler logs for that window, specifically looking for an exception around when the SLA callback should have fired. In my experience the most common reason an SLA alert doesn't fire even though sla= and the callback are both configured is that the callback itself errored out -- a dead webhook, an expired token -- and Airflow just doesn't make that failure loud anywhere except the scheduler log.

I'd also sanity-check that the scheduler itself was healthy that night and not backlogged or restarted in a way that could've caused it to skip an SLA evaluation cycle, and double check the SLA was actually attached to the task I think it was. But honestly, regardless of which of those turns out to be the specific cause, I'd come out of this pushing for an independent freshness check on the dashboard's data -- something that doesn't go through Airflow's SLA plumbing at all -- because a single alerting path for something a VP is looking at every morning isn't enough.
commonMistakes: Assuming an SLA miss alert is guaranteed to fire just because sla= is set
Not checking whether the sla_miss_callback itself threw an exception
Confusing SLA timing (scheduler-evaluated, DAG-run-relative) with simple task wall-clock duration
Relying on a single alerting mechanism for a business-critical pipeline
Not checking scheduler health/logs as the first troubleshooting step
keyPoints: SLA checks run on a scheduler loop, not from the task itself -- scheduler health matters
A failing sla_miss_callback can silently swallow the alert
Scheduler logs for that window are the highest-value first check
Verify the DAG wasn't paused or affected by catchup
Add an independent backstop freshness check for business-critical pipelines

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the SLA checking mechanism (scheduler-driven)
Identifies callback failure as a likely silent cause
Checks scheduler health/logs as a first step
Recommends an independent backstop monitoring mechanism
Clear overall explanation

questions.title: A dbt Test Failure Is Blocking a Production Deploy During Slim CI
questions.prompt: Your slim CI pipeline runs dbt build --select state:modified+ on every pull request. A PR that only renames a column in a staging model is now failing CI because a not_null test fails on a completely different downstream model that the PR author insists they didn't touch. How do you investigate, and what's the most likely explanation given how state:modified+ works?
questions.modelAnswer:
state:modified+ includes the renamed staging model plus everything downstream of it, because the + extends the selection to dependents -- so the "unrelated" failing model isn't actually unrelated; it got pulled into this CI run specifically because it's downstream of the renamed column. The first investigation step is confirming that dependency path with dbt ls --select state:modified+ or the lineage view, to see exactly how the failing model connects back to the renamed staging model.

The most likely explanation: the column rename broke a reference somewhere downstream that wasn't updated in lockstep -- a model still referencing the old column name via a wildcard select resolves silently to NULL for every row, or a join that depended on the old column name now produces unmatched rows that end up NULL on a required field. Either way, this is slim CI doing exactly what it's designed to do -- catching a downstream break before merge -- not a false positive, and the right fix is updating every downstream reference to the renamed column, not skipping the test or merging around it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd tell the PR author is: "you didn't touch that model, but state:modified+ includes everything downstream of what you did touch, so it's in this run for a reason." I'd pull up the lineage with dbt ls --select state:modified+ to actually trace how the failing model connects to the renamed column.

My bet, before even looking, is that the rename broke a downstream reference that didn't get updated -- maybe a model doing a select * that was quietly relying on the old column name, or a join key that silently produces nulls now that the name's changed. This isn't CI being flaky or over-eager -- it's catching exactly the kind of downstream breakage slim CI exists to catch. I'd have the author trace and fix the broken reference, not disable the test to get the PR through.
commonMistakes: Assuming a test failure on a model the PR author 'didn't touch' must be a CI bug or false positive
Not checking lineage to see the actual dependency path from the renamed column to the failing model
Disabling or skipping the failing test to force the merge through
Not understanding that state:modified+ intentionally includes downstream dependents, which is the point of slim CI
Treating a caught regression as noise instead of exactly the signal CI is designed to produce
keyPoints: state:modified+ pulls in downstream dependents, so seemingly unrelated models in the diff usually aren't
Use dbt ls/lineage to trace the actual dependency path
A column rename breaking a downstream reference is the most common real cause
This is CI working correctly, not a false positive
Fix the broken downstream reference rather than bypassing the test

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why + includes downstream dependents
Recommends tracing the actual lineage/dependency path
Identifies the renamed-column-breaking-downstream-reference as the likely cause
Does not recommend skipping/disabling the test as the fix

questions.title: An Airflow DAG Triggering a dbt Cloud Job Shows Success, but the Job Actually Failed
questions.prompt: You have an Airflow DAG that calls the dbt Cloud API to kick off a job via a trigger-and-poll pattern, then proceeds to a downstream Snowflake grants task. This morning the DAG shows all green, but the dbt Cloud job itself shows a failed run with several model errors. Diagnose how a failing dbt job could look like a successful Airflow task, and what you'd check in the Airflow operator's configuration.
questions.modelAnswer:
The most common cause is that a custom or legacy trigger-and-poll implementation only checked that the dbt Cloud API call to trigger the run was accepted (an HTTP 200-level response) and that the polling loop itself completed without an HTTP error -- without ever inspecting the dbt Cloud run's own terminal status field. A run can be successfully triggered and successfully polled to completion from the API's perspective while the underlying dbt job ends in error -- those are two different success signals, and conflating them is exactly what produces a green Airflow task over a red dbt Cloud run.

The fix is to use (or, if stuck with custom code, replicate the behavior of) the official Airflow dbt Cloud provider's DbtCloudRunJobOperator, which polls the run and explicitly raises an AirflowException if the run's terminal status isn't success, rather than succeeding on any non-error HTTP response. Also check whether wait_for_termination was actually set to True and whether the timeout was generous enough that the task didn't just stop polling early and assume success by default.

Add a downstream safeguard: an explicit check task that queries the dbt Cloud run's status via the API before the Snowflake grants task runs, so grants never get applied on top of models that may not have actually rebuilt.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This is almost always the same root cause: whatever's calling the dbt Cloud API checked "did the trigger call succeed" and "did polling finish without an HTTP error," but never actually looked at the dbt Cloud run's own status field. A job can fail completely and still look like a clean API interaction the whole way through, if nothing's checking that specific status.

I'd check two things in the operator config: is this using the official DbtCloudRunJobOperator, which actually raises on job failure, or some custom glue code that doesn't check status -- and is wait_for_termination actually set to True with a timeout long enough to let the real result come back. Either way, I'd add a check before the Snowflake grants task runs, so grants never get applied against models that may not have actually rebuilt successfully.
commonMistakes: Equating 'the API call succeeded' with 'the triggered job succeeded'
Using a custom trigger that doesn't check the dbt Cloud run's terminal status code
Not setting wait_for_termination or an adequate timeout
Letting a downstream task (grants, in this case) run against data that may not have refreshed, because nothing validated the real outcome

questions.title: Terraform Apply Fails With 'Resource Already Exists' After a Manual Incident Fix
questions.prompt: During an incident last week, an engineer manually created a storage account and a couple of firewall rules directly in the Azure Portal to restore service quickly, without updating the Terraform code or state for the shared data-platform environment. Nobody has touched the Terraform configuration for those resources since. Today's terraform apply for that environment fails with Azure errors that the storage account and firewall rules already exist. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and safely bring Terraform back in sync, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd read the actual error carefully first: an Azure 'already exists' or conflict error on an apply, for a resource that terraform plan showed as 'will be created' rather than 'will be updated,' is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change -- the real resource exists in Azure, but Terraform's state has no record of it, so Terraform tries to create it from scratch and Azure's own uniqueness constraints reject the duplicate.

I'd confirm the drift explicitly rather than assume it: run terraform plan and verify the affected resources show as '+ create,' and cross-reference the resource names/IDs from the error against what's actually visible via az resource show or the Portal. In this case that directly confirms the incident-week manual resources are the cause.

Structurally, this happens because Terraform state is only ever updated by Terraform itself -- through apply, import, or refresh. Any resource created directly through the Portal, the CLI, or by an engineer bypassing Terraform is completely invisible to the state file no matter how long it's existed, and a plan has no way to discover it on its own; it only compares the configuration against what's already recorded in state.

The fix is terraform import. For each drifted resource, I'd get its real Azure resource ID (az resource show --name ... --resource-group ... --resource-type ... --query id) and run terraform import <resource_address_in_config> <azure_resource_id> to attach the real object into state under the matching address. This requires a resource block already existing in the .tf configuration for that address -- import only binds state, it doesn't generate configuration, unless using Terraform's newer import block with -generate-config-out, which can scaffold a starting config from the real resource if the .tf code doesn't exist yet.

After importing, I'd immediately run terraform plan again -- this is the step people skip. Import only syncs the state's existence record; it says nothing about whether the .tf configuration's attributes actually match what was configured manually during the incident (for example, a firewall rule's IP range might differ from what's in code). The follow-up plan will show any genuine attribute drift as an '~ update,' which has to be reconciled deliberately: either update the .tf code to match the real, intentional incident configuration, or apply to bring the resource back to the originally-intended configuration, depending on which is actually correct going forward.

Beyond the immediate fix, I'd treat this as a process signal: if manual changes during an incident are sometimes unavoidable, build a habit or runbook step of importing them back into Terraform (or at minimum filing a ticket to do so) right after the incident closes, rather than discovering the drift weeks later at the next unrelated apply.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The error message itself tells me almost everything before I look at anything else -- Azure saying a resource 'already exists' on something Terraform's plan wanted to create, not update, is basically the textbook signature of state drift. Something real exists out there that Terraform's state file has simply never heard of.

I wouldn't just assume that, though -- I'd run plan and actually look at whether it's showing a '+ create' for those resources, and cross-check the names against what's genuinely sitting in the Portal or az resource show. In this case that's trivial to confirm, because we already know exactly what happened: someone created these by hand in the Portal during last week's incident, and nothing about that touched Terraform's code or state.

The mechanical reason this happens is worth being precise about: Terraform's state file only ever gets updated by Terraform itself. It has no way to notice, on its own, that a human created something matching its configuration out-of-band -- it just compares its config against whatever it already has on record, and if there's no record, its only option is to try to create it, which collides with the real one that's already there.

So the fix is terraform import -- get the real Azure resource ID, point it at the matching resource address in the .tf config, and import binds the two together in state. The part I'd be careful not to skip is what comes right after: import only fixes the fact that Terraform now knows the resource exists. It says nothing about whether the configuration in code actually matches what got configured by hand during the incident. So the very next thing is another plan, and whatever shows up as an update this time -- maybe a firewall rule's IP range doesn't match -- is a deliberate decision to make: update the code to reflect the real, intentional incident fix, or apply to bring it back to what was originally intended. Either is fine, but it has to be a decision, not an accident. And longer-term, I'd push for a habit of importing incident-time manual changes back into Terraform right away, rather than discovering this kind of drift at the next unrelated apply weeks later.
questions.example:
# Get the real Azure resource ID
az storage account show --name stdataplat01 --resource-group rg-data-platform --query id -o tsv

# Bind it into state at the matching config address
terraform import azurerm_storage_account.data_platform \
  /subscriptions/xxxx/resourceGroups/rg-data-platform/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stdataplat01

# ALWAYS re-plan after import to catch attribute-level drift
terraform plan

Deleting the manually-created Azure resources to let Terraform recreate them cleanly, discarding the incident fix
Running terraform import without first confirming via plan which specific resources/attributes are actually drifted
Treating import as a complete fix and not re-running plan afterward to catch attribute-level drift
Importing into the wrong resource address, not matching an existing/correct resource block, causing a different drift
keyPoints: 'Already exists' on a planned create, not an update, is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change
Terraform state only changes via Terraform itself; manually-created resources are invisible to it until explicitly imported
terraform import attaches an existing real resource to a state address but requires a matching config block (or the import block with -generate-config-out)
Import only fixes existence tracking -- a follow-up plan is required to catch and reconcile attribute-level drift
Process takeaway: import out-of-band incident changes back into Terraform promptly, not weeks later

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);

Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table

questions.title: Designing Dynamic RLS for 40 Sales Territories
questions.prompt: A company has 40 sales territories, each with its own manager who should only see their own territory's data, and the territory list changes periodically as the business reorganizes. Design the row-level security approach - don't just name the feature, walk through the actual model changes, the role definition, and how you'd validate it before any real manager is assigned.
questions.modelAnswer: Forty territories rules out a static role per value immediately - that's 40 roles to create and maintain by hand every time the org chart changes, and someone has to remember to add a 41st when the business adds a territory. The right design is a single dynamic role whose filter expression adapts to whoever is signed in, backed by a small user-mapping table added to the model: two columns, UserEmail and TerritoryID, with one row per manager, related to the territory dimension. The role's DAX filter expression is simply [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() on that mapping table - one role, one expression, scaling to any number of territories because the filtering logic never changes, only the rows in the mapping table do. A critical detail: USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() return different formats depending on where the report runs - USERNAME() returns DOMAIN\username in Desktop but a UPN in the service, while USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns a UPN-style value, like an email, in both places. Whichever function the role uses, the mapping table's values have to match the format that function actually returns when the report is viewed in the Power BI service, which is where real managers will view it, not necessarily what it shows while testing in Desktop. Before assigning a single real person, I'd validate with Test as role: select the role, confirm the report filters down to exactly one territory's data, and check that it matches the identity shown under 'Now viewing as.' The real limitation to flag: Test as role evaluates the filter using my own identity, so USERPRINCIPALNAME() inside the test returns my UPN, not the UPN of the manager I'm trying to simulate - it genuinely proves the filter logic works, but it can't prove a specific external manager will see the right data once onboarded. For that, the manager has to actually sign in and view it themselves, which I'd do for at least one real manager as a final check before rolling the role out to all 40.
questions.professionalAnswer: With 40 territories, I wouldn't even consider a static role per value - that's 40 things to build and maintain, and it falls apart the moment the org reorganizes. I'd build one dynamic role instead, backed by a small user-mapping table I add to the model: a UserEmail column and a TerritoryID column, related to the territory dimension, with one row per manager. The role's filter is just [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), and because that's the only logic, adding or removing a territory becomes a data update to the mapping table, not a model or role change. The detail I'd be careful about is that USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() don't necessarily return the same format in Desktop as they do once published to the service, so whichever function I pick, I need the mapping table's values to match what that function actually returns in the service, since that's where managers will really view it. Before putting a single real person on this, I'd use Test as role to confirm the filter narrows down to one territory correctly - but I'd be upfront that Test as role is checking the logic using my own identity, not proving what an actual colleague will see, so I'd still have at least one real manager sign in and verify their own view before rolling this out to all 40.
questions.example: Mapping table: UserMapping(UserEmail, TerritoryID) with 40 rows, one per manager, related to DimTerritory[TerritoryID]. Role 'Territory Manager' filter: [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Reorg handling: adding/removing a territory is an UPDATE to UserMapping, not a change to the role or the model.

Assuming USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() return the same format in Desktop and the service
Treating a successful Test as role result as proof a specific external manager will see correct data
Forgetting the mapping table needs a real relationship to the territory data for the filter to actually propagate

USERPRINCIPALNAME()/USERNAME() format must match what's stored in the mapping table as seen in the service

questions.title: Designing RLS for Managers With Overlapping, Combined Roles
questions.prompt: You need to design row-level security for a sales model where regional managers see only their own region, a few global executives should see everything, some category managers need their category across every region, and a handful of people hold combined roles - for example, a regional manager who is also a category manager somewhere else. How do you architect the RLS model, and what specific risks do you design around?
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd avoid creating a static role per combination of region and category - that approach doesn't scale and gets unmanageable the moment a second combined-access person shows up. Instead I'd build a small, data-driven entitlement table (UserEmail, AccessType, AccessValue) that lives outside the model, ideally synced from an HR or identity source, and define only a handful of roles in the model itself - Regional, Category, and Global - each with a DAX filter expression that checks this entitlement table via USERPRINCIPALNAME() rather than hardcoding a role per manager. Adding or removing someone's access then becomes a data change in the entitlement table, not a model redeploy.

The specific risk I design around hardest is that Power BI unions permissions across every role a user belongs to rather than intersecting them - so a regional manager who is also a category manager elsewhere needs to be deliberately tested to confirm they see exactly the union of their region plus their category, and nothing broader. I'd also explicitly design around the workspace-role bypass: RLS only applies to Viewer-level or app access, so any of these managers who also happen to have Contributor or Admin rights on the workspace would see everything regardless of role assignment, which has to be prevented by workspace access policy, not by anything in the DAX. For global executives, I'd use an explicit AllAccess flag in the entitlement table rather than a hardcoded unrestricted role, since that's easier to audit later. Finally, I'd treat this as an ongoing governance process rather than a one-time build - a periodic access review of the entitlement table, and mandatory testing of every combined-role scenario as part of UAT before go-live, since RLS is a security control and deserves the same rigor as one.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct is to not build a role for every possible combination of region and category, because that's a maintenance nightmare the second someone's access changes. I'd build a small entitlement table outside the model - who gets what region, category, or global access - and have just a few DAX roles that look that table up dynamically, so changing someone's access is a data edit, not a model change. The thing I'd specifically test hardest, because it bites people constantly, is that Power BI doesn't intersect multiple roles - it unions them. So that regional-manager-who's-also-a-category-manager-elsewhere has to be verified to see exactly region-plus-category and nothing more, not some unexpected broader combination. I'd also make sure none of these managers have Contributor or Admin rights on the workspace, because RLS just doesn't apply to those roles regardless of how carefully I've built the DAX - that's a workspace-permissions conversation, not a modeling one. And for the global executives, I'd rather give them an explicit flag in the entitlement table than a separate 'sees everything' role, just because it's easier to audit later who actually has that kind of access and why.

Not explicitly testing combined-role users before go-live

questions.title: Designing a Code-Review Workflow for Power BI Report Changes
questions.prompt: Six analysts all edit the same set of Power BI reports and the shared semantic model directly in the Service, and changes occasionally break visuals or measures for everyone with no review step. Leadership wants a Git-based review process. Describe the workflow, and be honest about the real constraints you have to design around given that Power BI content isn't naturally diffable text.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first and most important move is getting off the traditional .pbix binary format for anything that's going to live under Git review, and onto the Power BI Project (.pbip) format, which serializes the report layout and the semantic model as readable JSON/TMDL folders instead of an opaque binary - without that change, 'Git-based review' is really just file storage, since a binary diff tells a reviewer nothing. With .pbip in place, the workflow looks like normal software development: analysts work on feature branches in Desktop, commit their .pbip changes, and open a pull request; reviewers read the TMDL/JSON diff to understand exactly what measures or model relationships changed, and also open the branch in Desktop to visually check the report before approving, since even a text-diffable model format doesn't make a changed chart layout meaningfully reviewable as text. Branch protection requires at least one approval before merge, and promotion from Dev to Test to Production workspaces happens through a deployment pipeline (Power BI Deployment Pipelines, or a scripted deploy via the Fabric/Power BI REST API in a CI job) triggered only from the main branch - never a direct publish from someone's Desktop straight into Production.

I'd be upfront with leadership about the real limits here: visual/layout changes are still genuinely hard to review as a diff even in TMDL format, so reviewers need to actually open and look at the report, not just read JSON; and the same report being edited on two branches at once is still a painful, mostly-manual merge conflict to resolve, since this isn't line-based collaborative text editing the way code is. This also requires a real culture shift for analysts used to live-editing in the Service - I'd recommend keeping a separate 'self-service sandbox' workspace where ad hoc, ungoverned edits are still fine, and reserving the Git-reviewed workflow specifically for the curated, widely-consumed production reports and the shared semantic model, rather than trying to force every edit through PR review.
questions.professionalAnswer: Step one, honestly, is getting everyone off .pbix and onto the .pbip project format, because a binary file in Git is basically just backup storage - nobody can meaningfully review a diff of it. Once we're on .pbip, this starts to look like a normal PR workflow: branch, commit, open a pull request, and a reviewer can actually read the TMDL diff to see what measure or relationship changed, plus open it in Desktop to eyeball the visual layout before approving. I'd set up branch protection requiring at least one approval, and route Dev-to-Test-to-Prod promotion through a deployment pipeline triggered from main, not someone manually publishing from their own machine. But I'd tell leadership straight up that this isn't going to be as clean as reviewing code - layout and visual changes still need an actual human look, not just a JSON diff, and if two people touch the same report on different branches at the same time, that merge conflict is still going to be painful to resolve. And this is as much a habit change as a tooling change, so I'd keep a separate sandbox workspace where people can still just edit live for quick personal stuff, and reserve this whole governed process for the reports that actually matter broadly.

questions.title: A CI/CD Strategy Spanning dbt, T-SQL, and Power BI
questions.prompt: Your analytics stack has dbt models, hand-written T-SQL stored procedures, and Power BI semantic models, all needing to move safely from dev to test to production. Design an end-to-end CI/CD strategy covering all three, including what runs automatically on every pull request versus what requires manual promotion.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd put all three codebases under Git with environment-specific configuration externalized rather than hardcoded - dbt profiles/targets per environment, SQL Server connection strings pulled from Key Vault, and Power BI deployment pipeline stages - so the same code behaves correctly wherever it's promoted to. On every pull request, CI runs a consistent set of automatic, required-to-pass gates: dbt build and test against an ephemeral or shared dev schema to validate models and data tests, T-SQL changes get run through lightweight tests (tSQLt unit tests, or a script executing procs against a test database and asserting expected results) plus SQL linting, and for Power BI, if the team has adopted .pbip/TMDL, a model validation step using something like Tabular Editor's command-line best-practice-analyzer rules or a basic schema diff. None of this touches Test or Production directly; it only validates the PR before merge.

Manual promotion is reserved specifically for Test and Production deployment. Merging to main can trigger automatic deployment to Test, but Production promotion requires an explicit human approval gate - GitHub Environments with required reviewers, or someone manually triggering the Power BI Deployment Pipeline's production stage - because a bad semantic model refresh or schema change can break dashboards people are actively using, and that deserves a deliberate, business-hours-aware human decision rather than full automation. I'd also insist on versioned migration scripts for T-SQL changes rather than ad hoc proc edits directly in Production, so database schema changes get the same promotion discipline as everything else, and I'd keep all secrets in Key Vault or GitHub Secrets with least-privilege, environment-scoped credentials rather than anywhere in the repository itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat all three - dbt, T-SQL, and Power BI - as needing the same basic promotion discipline, even though the specific checks look different for each. On every PR, I want automatic, required checks: dbt build and test against a dev schema, some kind of T-SQL test (even lightweight tSQLt tests or a script that runs the procs and checks results) plus a linter, and if we're on .pbip for Power BI, a model validation pass. None of that touches anything beyond dev, it's just the gate before merge. Where I'd deliberately slow things down is Production - merging to main can auto-deploy to Test, but Production needs an actual human to approve the promotion, especially for the Power BI semantic model, because breaking a live dashboard refresh is a very different kind of incident than a failed dev build. I'd also make sure T-SQL changes go through versioned migration scripts instead of someone editing a proc directly in Prod, so the database gets the same rigor as the code, and obviously none of the connection strings or API keys live anywhere but Key Vault or GitHub Secrets, scoped tightly per environment.

Automatically deploying production-impacting changes without a human approval gate
Not testing T-SQL changes at all because there's no dbt-equivalent test framework assumed
Storing credentials/connection strings in repo configuration instead of a secrets manager
Not distinguishing automatic PR-gate checks from deliberate, approved Production promotion
