questions.title: Resolving a Disagreement Over Who Owns the Definition of 'Active Customer'
questions.prompt: The metric active_customer_count is defined in your dbt semantic layer, but the Marketing analytics team built their own version in a spreadsheet that's been circulating for a year and gives a different number. Marketing's VP is now quoting their number in a board deck. How do you resolve this without it becoming a turf war?
questions.modelAnswer:
Start by understanding the actual logic difference before asserting the dbt definition is "right" -- the spreadsheet version likely encodes a real business judgment (a different activity window, excluding trial accounts) that may be legitimate rather than simply wrong, and approaching this as "my number is correct, yours is wrong" guarantees a turf war regardless of who's technically right. Set up a working session with whoever owns the spreadsheet logic to diff the two definitions line by line and surface where they actually diverge.

If the spreadsheet's logic reflects a genuine, still-relevant business decision, incorporate it into the governed metric -- potentially as a named variant if the two audiences genuinely need different definitions -- rather than forcing one-size-fits-all. If it's simply stale or based on a misunderstanding, present the reconciliation findings neutrally and let the VP decide which number to use going forward, rather than unilaterally overriding an already-public number. Either way, end with exactly one governed definition both teams commit to using, with the reconciliation documented so it doesn't resurface next quarter.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move isn't "our number is right" -- it's figuring out what's actually different about the two calculations. Marketing's spreadsheet has probably been circulating for a year because it captures something real about how they think about "active," even if it's not how we defined it. I'd sit down with whoever owns that spreadsheet and diff the logic line by line.

If their version turns out to reflect a real, still-valid business distinction, I'd fold that into the governed metric, maybe as a clearly named variant if both groups genuinely need different numbers. If it's just stale, I'd present that neutrally to the VP rather than telling her she's wrong in a meeting -- it's her call which number she uses going forward, not mine to unilaterally override. Either way, I want us to walk away with one governed number everybody's agreed to use, written down somewhere so this doesn't happen again next quarter.
commonMistakes: Assuming the dbt-defined metric is automatically correct just because it's the governed one
Approaching the conversation as a technical correctness contest rather than a logic reconciliation
Unilaterally telling a VP their already-public number is wrong instead of presenting a neutral reconciliation
Resolving it informally/verbally without documenting the reconciled definition, letting the conflict resurface
Not considering that two genuinely different, legitimate definitions might both need to exist as clearly-named variants
keyPoints: Diagnose the actual logic difference before assuming either definition is simply wrong
Treat this as a reconciliation, not a correctness contest, to avoid a turf war
Involve the right stakeholder in the final decision rather than unilaterally overriding a public number
Consider whether two legitimate, clearly-named metric variants are warranted
Document the reconciled definition so the disagreement doesn't resurface

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Investigates the actual logic difference before asserting correctness
Frames the conversation as reconciliation rather than a turf war
Involves the appropriate stakeholder in the final decision
Documents/governs the resolved definition going forward

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Analytics Engineer Through Their First Incremental Model
questions.prompt: A junior analytics engineer on your team is about to convert their first model from a full-refresh table to incremental, and you can tell from their PR description they don't yet have an intuition for what can go wrong (idempotency, late-arriving data, the first-run edge case). How do you mentor them through this without just rewriting their PR yourself?
questions.modelAnswer:
Resist the urge to just fix the PR directly, since that solves this one model but doesn't build the junior engineer's intuition for the next ten they'll write. Instead, ask a sequence of questions in the PR review that lead them to the gaps themselves: "What happens if this job runs twice in a row on the same day?" "What's the oldest updated_at a genuinely new row to this run could have -- does your filter window account for that?" "What happens the very first time this model runs, before the table exists at all?"

Pair with them to actually run the edge cases together -- trigger a double-run in a dev schema and look at the row counts, deliberately inject a late-arriving row outside their filter window and watch it get dropped -- so the lesson comes from observed behavior, not a lecture. Afterwards, suggest writing a short internal checklist for the team's next incremental model PR, turning a one-on-one mentoring moment into a durable team asset.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just rewrite their PR -- that fixes this one model and teaches them nothing for the next one. I'd ask questions in the review instead: what happens if this runs twice back to back on the same day, what's the oldest a genuinely new row could be and does your window cover that, what happens the very first time this runs before the table even exists.

Then I'd actually sit with them and run it -- trigger a double run in a dev schema and look at what happens to the row counts, feed in a late row on purpose and watch it get dropped by their filter. Seeing it break is a lot stickier than being told it would break. And afterward I'd have them turn what we found into a short checklist for the team's next incremental PR, so the lesson doesn't just live in their head -- it becomes something the team actually uses.
commonMistakes: Rewriting the junior engineer's PR directly instead of guiding them to find the issues themselves
Lecturing about incremental model theory in the abstract instead of walking through this model's actual edge cases
Not actually demonstrating the failure modes hands-on, relying only on verbal explanation
Treating this as a one-off correction instead of turning it into a reusable team checklist
Being overly critical in the PR review instead of using guided questions
keyPoints: Guide with targeted questions rather than rewriting the PR, to build lasting intuition
Focus on the specific real edge cases: idempotency, late data, first run
Demonstrate failure modes hands-on in a dev environment rather than only describing them
Turn the mentoring moment into a durable team artifact
Balance correction with respect for the junior engineer's growth

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses guided questions/dialogue rather than directly rewriting the PR
Identifies and addresses the specific relevant edge cases
Demonstrates or proposes hands-on verification rather than only verbal explanation
Proposes turning the lesson into a durable team artifact

questions.title: Negotiating Test Coverage Requirements Before a Deploy
questions.prompt: A product manager wants a new revenue dashboard shipped by Friday. The underlying dbt models are ready, but you've only had time to add not_null tests, not the relationships and custom business-logic tests you'd normally want on anything revenue-related. The PM says "ship it, we'll add tests later." How do you handle this negotiation?
questions.modelAnswer:
Don't treat this as a binary ship-with-no-tests-vs-miss-the-deadline choice. Reframe it as a risk conversation with specific, named risks rather than a vague "testing is good practice" objection: "without a relationships test between fct_revenue and dim_customer, an orphaned foreign key will silently show as $0 or blank instead of erroring, and because this is revenue, that's the kind of number a VP might quote before anyone notices it's wrong."

Propose a scoped compromise rather than all-or-nothing: ship Friday with not_null plus the one or two highest-risk tests that are fast to add -- a relationships test and a reasonableness check against last week's total -- and get explicit agreement on a specific date for the remaining tests, ideally as a tracked follow-up ticket with the PM's name on it. If the PM still insists on zero additional tests, document the decision and its risk so that if a data quality issue surfaces, it's a known, accepted trade-off rather than an oversight -- not to assign blame, but so the next negotiation starts from evidence instead of zero.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just comply with zero extra tests, and I wouldn't refuse to ship either. I'd get specific about the actual risk: "if there's an orphaned customer record, this will show as a blank or zero instead of erroring, and that's a number someone might quote to a VP before we catch it." That lands very differently than "testing is best practice."

Then I'd propose a middle ground -- I can add the relationships test and a sanity check against last week's number before Friday, those are fast, and I want a specific date, not 'later,' for the rest. If the PM still says no additional tests at all, I'd write that decision down somewhere visible, not to cover myself after the fact, but so if something does go wrong, we're having the next conversation from "here's what happened last time" instead of starting from scratch.
commonMistakes: Either silently complying with zero tests or refusing to ship at all, instead of negotiating a scoped middle ground
Arguing for testing in the abstract instead of naming the specific, concrete risk to this exact dashboard
Agreeing to 'add tests later' with no specific date or ticket, which in practice usually means never
Not documenting the accepted risk/trade-off, leaving the engineer exposed if something breaks
Not identifying which one or two tests would catch the highest-risk failure modes cheaply
keyPoints: Reframe the ask as specific, named risk rather than abstract best practice
Propose a scoped compromise instead of all-or-nothing
Secure a concrete, committed follow-up rather than an open-ended 'later'
Document the accepted trade-off so it's a known decision, not an invisible gap
Focus on the highest-leverage tests given limited time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Reframes the risk concretely rather than arguing abstract best practice
Proposes a scoped middle-ground compromise instead of all-or-nothing
Secures a concrete, committed follow-up rather than an open-ended 'later'
Documents the accepted trade-off

questions.title: Owning an Incident Where a Loose dbt Test Threshold Let Bad Data Reach Dashboards
questions.prompt: A dbt test you wrote last quarter checks that daily order volume doesn't drop more than 50% day-over-day. Last week, a real upstream bug cut order volume by 40%, which passed your test and reached the executive dashboard, leading to a confusing week of decisions based on wrong numbers before someone caught it manually. The bug is now fixed. How do you handle owning this in the team retro?
questions.modelAnswer:
Own the threshold decision directly and specifically rather than being vague or defensive: "I set that test's threshold at 50% last quarter based on the historical day-of-week swings I'd seen at the time, and it turned out too loose for this kind of failure -- that's on me to recalibrate." Avoid over-correcting into blame-free vagueness that teaches nothing, or excessive self-flagellation that makes the retro about feelings instead of the fix.

Bring a concrete proposal, not just an apology: tighten the threshold using actual historical variance data -- a statistical bound like 2-3 standard deviations from the trailing 90-day daily volume rather than a round guessed number -- and propose a second, faster-acting check specifically for anything feeding the executive dashboard, since a once-a-night test already means up to 24 hours of exposure even with a perfect threshold. Separately, raise the process gap exposed by "someone caught it manually after a week" -- the detection delay is its own problem worth fixing independent of the specific number being wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd own it directly: I set that 50% threshold last quarter based on the day-of-week swings I'd seen at the time, and it turned out too loose for this kind of drop. That's a calibration mistake, and it's mine to fix -- I'm not going to be vague about it, and I'm also not going to turn the retro into me beating myself up, because that doesn't help anyone.

What I'd actually bring is a fix: recalculate the threshold off real variance in the trailing 90 days instead of a number I guessed, and propose something tighter and faster specifically for whatever feeds the exec dashboard, since even a perfect nightly test still leaves up to a day of exposure. And separately, I'd flag that it took a week for someone to catch this manually -- that's its own gap worth fixing regardless of what the threshold ends up being.
commonMistakes: Being vague or defensive about the threshold decision instead of owning the specific number and reasoning
Treating the retro as either a blame session or a no-fault shrug, both of which skip the learning
Proposing only to 'tighten the threshold' without concrete historical data to justify the new value
Not addressing the week-long detection gap as its own separate problem from the threshold itself
Not proposing anything specifically for dashboards with executive visibility, where exposure time matters more
keyPoints: Own the specific decision and reasoning directly, neither defensively nor with excessive self-blame
Bring a concrete, data-backed proposal to fix the threshold
Recognize the detection-time gap as a separate, systemic problem worth solving independently
Propose tighter/faster safeguards specifically for executive-facing dashboards
Use the retro to drive both the specific fix and the broader process improvement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Owns the specific past decision directly without being defensive or overly self-blaming
Proposes a concrete, data-backed fix to the threshold
Identifies and addresses the broader detection-time/process gap separately
Distinguishes the needs of executive-facing dashboards from a general data quality bar

questions.title: Getting a Resistant Team to Adopt Slim CI
questions.prompt: You want your team to switch from "run the full dbt build manually before merging" to automated Slim CI on every PR. Two senior engineers on the team are resistant -- they feel it adds process overhead and don't trust automated checks over "just looking at the diff." How do you get buy-in rather than mandating it top-down?
questions.modelAnswer:
Start from genuinely understanding the resistance rather than assuming it's stubbornness -- "just looking at the diff" has likely caught real problems for these engineers before, and dismissing that experience outright will make them dig in further. Address the actual concern with evidence rather than a mandate: pick a recent real incident where manual review missed a downstream break that Slim CI's state:modified+ selection would have caught, or construct a realistic example from the project's actual dependency graph, and show it concretely rather than arguing in the abstract.

Propose a low-stakes trial rather than an all-at-once switch: run Slim CI alongside the existing manual process for a few weeks, so skeptics can watch it run without yet being forced to trust it exclusively, and compare notes on what it catches versus manual review in that window. Give the resistant engineers a real voice in the rollout specifics -- which checks are required, whether certain changes still get an extra manual look -- rather than presenting it as a finished decision, since ownership over the details often converts "this was imposed on us" into "we built this."
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just mandate it -- I'd first actually ask why they're skeptical, because "just looking at the diff" has probably caught real things for them before, and brushing that off is a fast way to make them dig in harder. I'd find a real case, or build a realistic one from our own dependency graph, where a manual review missed something state:modified+ would have caught, and show it concretely instead of arguing in the abstract.

Then I'd propose running it alongside the manual process for a few weeks rather than switching cold -- let them watch it work without being forced to trust it on day one. And I'd actually give them a say in how it's configured -- what's required to pass, whether some changes still get a manual look on top -- because people who help build the rollout are a lot more likely to actually use it than people who just had it handed to them.
commonMistakes: Mandating the change top-down without engaging with the specific source of resistance
Arguing for automation in the abstract instead of showing a concrete case where it would have caught something manual review missed
Switching over all at once instead of running a trial period that lets skeptics build trust incrementally
Not giving the resistant engineers any say in the rollout details
Dismissing 'just looking at the diff' as simply wrong, when it likely reflects real past experience
keyPoints: Understand the specific source of resistance rather than assuming simple stubbornness
Use a concrete real or realistic example showing what Slim CI would have caught
Propose a trial/parallel-run period rather than an all-at-once mandate
Involve the resistant engineers in shaping the rollout details
Acknowledge the legitimate value of their past experience rather than dismissing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Genuinely investigates/acknowledges the specific resistance rather than dismissing it
Uses a concrete example to demonstrate value rather than an abstract argument
Proposes an incremental trial rather than an all-at-once mandate
Involves the resistant engineers in shaping rollout details

questions.title: Collaborating With an Upstream Data Engineering Team When Their Schema Changes Break Your dbt Models
questions.prompt: The data engineering team that owns the raw/bronze layer feeding your dbt staging models keeps shipping schema changes (renamed columns, changed types) without notice, breaking your models at random times. They see this as "their" data and don't feel obligated to coordinate with analytics engineering. How do you fix this relationship, not just the immediate breaks?
questions.modelAnswer:
Start by understanding why the data engineering team doesn't feel obligated to coordinate -- often a genuine gap rather than indifference: they may not actually know which downstream models depend on which raw columns, so a change that looks internal-only to them is invisible-breaking to you. Make the dependency visible and concrete rather than arguing the principle: share dbt's own lineage/exposures showing exactly which staging models, and ultimately which dashboards, depend on their raw tables, so the conversation moves from "you should be nicer about this" to "here's the specific blast radius when column X changes without notice."

Propose a lightweight, low-friction coordination mechanism rather than demanding a heavy process they'll resist -- a shared Slack channel or a PR-tag convention where schema changes to tables with known downstream dependencies get a heads-up before merge. Add dbt source freshness checks and explicit schema tests on the sources so breaks surface immediately and specifically rather than as a confusing downstream model failure, protecting your side even on changes they genuinely forget to flag.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before assuming they just don't care, I'd check whether they actually know what depends on their tables -- a lot of the time this isn't indifference, it's that nobody's ever shown them the blast radius. I'd pull dbt's lineage and exposures and show them concretely: here's exactly which of our models, and which dashboards, break when this column changes without a heads-up.

Then instead of asking for a heavy approval process they're going to resist, I'd propose something light -- a shared channel, or a tag on their PRs when a change touches a table we depend on, just enough to get a heads-up before it merges. And on our side, I'd add source freshness and schema tests regardless of whether the coordination improves, so even when they do forget, we get a clear "column X is missing" error instead of a confusing downstream failure three models later.
commonMistakes: Approaching the data engineering team with blame rather than making the actual dependency and its cost visible
Demanding a heavy, bureaucratic change-approval process a resistant team will likely ignore
Only fixing the technical symptom without addressing the underlying coordination gap
Assuming the other team's lack of coordination is pure indifference rather than a visibility gap
Not proposing anything lightweight enough to actually get adopted
keyPoints: Diagnose whether the lack of coordination is indifference or a visibility gap about actual dependencies
Use dbt's lineage/exposures to make the concrete blast radius visible
Propose a lightweight coordination mechanism likely to actually get adopted
Add source freshness/schema tests as a technical safety net independent of whether coordination improves
Address both the relationship/process gap and the immediate technical exposure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Diagnoses the root cause of the coordination gap rather than assuming pure indifference
Uses concrete lineage/dependency evidence to make the case
Proposes a lightweight, realistically adoptable coordination mechanism
Adds a technical safety net independent of the relationship fix

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem on an Airflow Outage That Delayed a Board Report
questions.prompt: An Airflow scheduler outage overnight delayed the pipeline feeding a board-level report by six hours, and it was caught just in time before the board meeting. You're leading the postmortem. One engineer's weekend deploy is the proximate trigger. How do you run this so it's genuinely blameless but still produces real accountability and fixes?
questions.modelAnswer:
Blameless doesn't mean cause-less -- the postmortem should state plainly that a weekend deploy was the proximate trigger, without making that framing about the engineer as a person. Reframe the central question from "who caused this" to "what made it possible for one weekend deploy to take down the scheduler for six hours, and why didn't we catch it sooner" -- that reframing is what produces systemic fixes instead of a single person feeling punished while the underlying gaps repeat with a different engineer next time.

In the postmortem itself, explicitly invite the engineer who made the deploy to walk through their reasoning and what information they had at the time, since understanding why a reasonable person made that call under those conditions is more valuable than establishing "the deploy was the cause." Produce concrete action items with owners and dates -- a required review step for off-hours production deploys, scheduler health added to the paging rotation's monitored signals -- rather than ending with only a narrative, since a postmortem that doesn't change anything structurally is just a story people feel bad about.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Blameless doesn't mean we pretend we don't know what happened -- we say plainly that a weekend deploy was the trigger, but I keep the framing on the system, not the person. The question I'd actually run the meeting around is "what let one weekend deploy take the scheduler down for six hours, and why did it take us that long to notice," not "whose fault was this."

I'd specifically ask the engineer who made the deploy to walk through what they knew and why it seemed reasonable at the time, because that's more useful than just confirming they did it. And I wouldn't let the meeting end with just a good discussion -- I want actual action items with names and dates attached, like a required review step for off-hours deploys and getting scheduler health into our paging signals, because a postmortem that doesn't change anything is just a story everyone feels bad about.
commonMistakes: Conflating 'blameless' with 'not identifying what actually happened', producing a vague postmortem
Focusing the conversation on the individual engineer's decision instead of the systemic gaps
Not inviting the engineer to explain their actual reasoning/context
Ending the postmortem with only a narrative and no concrete, owned action items
Not addressing the detection delay as its own separate, equally important finding
keyPoints: Blameless means not punishing the person, not avoiding naming what actually happened
Reframe from 'who caused this' to 'what systemic gap let this happen and go undetected'
Invite the engineer involved to share their actual context/reasoning
The detection delay is its own separate systemic finding worth fixing
Close with concrete, owned, dated action items, not just a narrative

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blameless from avoiding the actual cause
Reframes toward systemic gaps rather than individual fault
Involves the engineer constructively to surface context, not blame
Produces concrete owned action items addressing both the trigger and the detection delay

questions.title: Making the Case for Investing in Test Coverage When Roadmap Pressure Favors New Features
questions.prompt: Your team's dbt project has grown to 200 models with test coverage concentrated almost entirely on a handful of old, well-known models -- most newer marts have little beyond not_null. Leadership's roadmap is entirely new-feature-driven for the next two quarters, and "go write more tests" isn't going to win a prioritization fight on its own. How do you actually get investment in this?
questions.modelAnswer:
Don't ask for "more test coverage" as a standalone initiative competing against named features for the same roadmap slots -- that framing almost always loses, since it's abstract against something concrete. Instead, attach testing investment to the roadmap leadership already cares about: identify which of the next two quarters' new features actually build on top of the under-tested marts, and reframe the ask as de-risking the foundation those specific upcoming features depend on, rather than general hygiene.

Bring data, not a feeling: a quick audit showing exactly which models have which test coverage, cross-referenced against which of those models feed this quarter's planned features or executive-visible dashboards, so the gap is visible and prioritized by actual business exposure. Propose a low-overhead mechanism that doesn't require a dedicated "testing quarter": require a baseline test as part of the Definition of Done for any model touched or built as part of a new feature, so coverage grows incrementally, funded by the feature work leadership already prioritized.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't pitch "we need more tests" as its own line item competing against named features -- that loses every time because it's abstract against something concrete. I'd figure out which of the next two quarters' actual planned features sit on top of the under-tested marts, and reframe the ask as de-risking the foundation those specific features depend on.

I'd back that with a quick audit -- here's test coverage by model, here's which of those feed this quarter's roadmap or the exec dashboards -- so it's not a vague feeling, it's a visible gap tied to real exposure. And instead of asking for a dedicated testing sprint, which competes for the same slots, I'd propose baking a baseline test requirement into the Definition of Done for any model touched as part of new feature work, so coverage grows as a byproduct of work leadership's already funding.
commonMistakes: Pitching 'more tests' as a standalone initiative that has to win a prioritization fight against named features
Treating all 200 models as equally under-tested rather than identifying which gaps actually expose upcoming roadmap work
Asking for a dedicated block of time that competes directly with the feature roadmap
Not having concrete audit data to show where the real exposure is
Missing the opportunity to attach a lightweight, durable mechanism that keeps growing coverage without repeated separate asks
keyPoints: Attach the testing ask to specific upcoming roadmap work rather than pitching it as a standalone initiative
Use a concrete audit to show where test coverage gaps overlap with business exposure
Frame it as de-risking the foundation leadership's own roadmap depends on
Propose a lightweight, incremental mechanism funded by existing feature work
Prioritize by actual exposure rather than treating all gaps equally

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Attaches the ask to specific roadmap-relevant exposure rather than pitching standalone coverage
Uses concrete audit data to identify and prioritize the real gaps
Proposes a lightweight, incremental mechanism rather than requiring a dedicated allocation
Demonstrates understanding of why 'go write more tests' alone fails as a pitch

questions.title: Moving a Portal-Clicking Team to Terraform/Bicep Over Skeptical Senior Pushback
questions.prompt: Your team has always provisioned Azure resources by clicking through the portal, and you want to move the team to Terraform/Bicep for a new data platform build. Two senior teammates are skeptical, citing 'it's slower than just clicking the thing I need' and past frustration with a previous team's over-engineered Terraform setup. How do you negotiate this adoption?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the skepticism as legitimate signal rather than resistance to be overcome by mandate. The candidate should start by separating the two objections, since they need different responses: 'portal is faster for a one-off' is often true and should be acknowledged honestly rather than argued away, while the past bad experience with over-engineered Terraform is a real scar that a new rollout needs to explicitly design against -- by keeping the initial module set small, flat, and genuinely necessary rather than building abstraction layers nobody asked for.

The candidate should propose an approach that lets the skeptics experience the value rather than being told about it: start with a new, lower-stakes piece of the platform build, let the team keep clicking for genuinely one-off exploratory resources for now, and bring the skeptics into writing the first modules rather than handing them a framework decided in isolation. The real argument for adoption -- consistent, reviewable, repeatable environments; drift detection; faster disaster recovery -- should be made concretely against this specific platform build's needs, not as an abstract best-practice argument, and the candidate should be honest that there's a real short-term velocity cost that pays off over the project's lifetime, not instantly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't go in trying to win an argument -- I'd go in treating their pushback as two separate, legitimate points that need different answers. 'Clicking is faster for the thing I need right now' is just true a lot of the time, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But 'the last Terraform setup I used was over-engineered and painful' is the one I actually need to address head-on, by being explicit that whatever we build this time starts small and flat -- no module-of-modules, no abstraction for things we don't have yet.

Practically, I'd rather let them feel the benefit than argue them into it. I'd pick a lower-stakes piece of the new platform build to go first, keep it genuinely simple, and actually have the two of them help write those first modules instead of handing them something I designed alone and asking them to adopt it. And I'd be straight with them that yes, this is going to be a bit slower than clicking for the first few weeks -- the payoff is in repeatable environments and not having to remember what we clicked six months from now when we need to rebuild something, and that's a real tradeoff, not a free win I'm selling them.
commonMistakes: Treating the skepticism as pure resistance to change instead of partially valid feedback
Arguing that Terraform is strictly faster, which isn't true for small one-off changes and damages credibility
Ignoring or dismissing the team's past bad experience with an over-engineered IaC setup instead of designing against it
Mandating the switch top-down without letting the skeptics co-author the first real modules
Overselling adoption as a free win instead of being honest about the short-term velocity cost
keyPoints: Separates the 'portal is faster' objection from the 'past over-engineering' objection and addresses each specifically
Explicitly designs the new rollout to be small and simple, directly countering the past bad experience
Lets skeptics experience the value on a real, lower-stakes piece of work rather than mandating from above
Involves the skeptical senior teammates in authoring the first modules
Is honest about the real short-term velocity tradeoff rather than overselling adoption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates and responds to the two distinct objections
Proposes a concrete plan to avoid repeating the past over-engineering experience
Involves the skeptical teammates directly rather than mandating adoption top-down
Makes a concrete, project-specific case for adoption rather than an abstract best-practices argument
Is honest about real tradeoffs instead of overselling the change

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem on a Terraform Apply That Took Down a Shared Event Hub
questions.prompt: A `terraform apply` run by a teammate, approved in a rushed review, took down a shared production Event Hub namespace for 40 minutes before anyone noticed. You're leading the blameless postmortem. How do you run it so it's genuinely blameless but still produces real accountability and fixes?
questions.modelAnswer:
Blameless does not mean avoiding naming what happened -- the postmortem should state plainly that a specific Terraform change, approved in a rushed review, triggered the outage, while keeping the framing on the system that allowed it rather than on the individuals as people. The candidate should reframe the central question from 'who broke the Event Hub' to 'what let a plan with this blast radius get approved in a rushed review, and why did it take 40 minutes to notice a shared production namespace was down.' That reframing is what produces durable fixes instead of two people -- the author and the reviewer -- feeling punished while the same gap exists for the next risky change.

The candidate should explicitly involve both the author and the reviewer in walking through their reasoning: what the plan output looked like, what time pressure existed, why the blast radius of the change (a shared resource used by other teams) wasn't flagged in review. The postmortem should close with concrete, owned, dated action items distinct from the individuals' behavior -- for example, requiring plan output to explicitly call out changes to shared/cross-team resources, a mandatory second reviewer or cooling-off period for changes touching shared infrastructure, and alerting on the Event Hub namespace's health so a future outage is caught in minutes, not 40.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Blameless doesn't mean we're vague about what happened -- I'll say directly that a specific apply, approved in a review that got rushed, is what took the namespace down. But I keep steering the room toward the system question: what let a change with this big a blast radius get approved quickly, and why did it take 40 minutes before anyone noticed a shared production resource was gone, rather than who personally messed up.

I'd ask both the person who wrote the change and the person who reviewed it to actually walk through their side -- what the plan output showed, what the time pressure looked like, whether anything flagged that this touched a resource other teams depend on. And I'm not going to let the meeting end as just a good conversation -- I want it to end with specific fixes: plan output that calls out changes to shared resources explicitly, maybe a required second reviewer or a short cooling-off window for anything touching shared infra, and health alerting on that namespace so next time we catch it in minutes instead of 40.
commonMistakes: Conflating 'blameless' with being vague about what actually happened or who was involved
Focusing on the individual author's or reviewer's judgment instead of the systemic review gap
Not inviting both the author and the reviewer to explain their actual context and reasoning
Treating the 40-minute detection delay as a footnote instead of an equally important separate finding
Ending with a narrative discussion but no concrete, owned, dated action items
keyPoints: States plainly what happened and who was involved without making it about individual blame
Reframes toward the systemic gap: why a high-blast-radius change cleared a rushed review
Involves both the author and reviewer constructively to surface real context
Treats the 40-minute detection delay as its own distinct, important finding
Closes with concrete, owned, dated action items covering both the review gap and detection gap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Distinguishes blameless from avoiding naming the actual cause and people involved
Reframes the discussion toward the systemic review gap rather than individual fault
Involves both author and reviewer constructively to surface context, not blame
Identifies the detection delay as a separate, equally important finding
Produces concrete, owned, dated action items addressing both gaps

questions.title: Justifying Terraform-Managed Snowflake Infrastructure to a Team That's Always Used Snowsight
questions.prompt: Your analytics team has always created Snowflake warehouses, roles, and resource monitors by clicking through Snowsight, and it works fine day to day. You want to move those definitions into Terraform using the Snowflake provider. The team's informal reaction is 'why would we add a deploy pipeline for something that takes two minutes in the UI?' How do you make the case, and what would you deliberately NOT move into code?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer doesn't argue that Terraform is faster than clicking — for a genuine one-off, it usually isn't, and claiming otherwise damages credibility. The real case is about what clicking through Snowsight can't give you over time: six months from now, nobody can reliably answer 'what warehouses, roles, and resource monitors exist and why,' RBAC grants accumulate ad hoc and are rarely revoked when someone changes teams, and a resource monitor someone disabled during an incident has no record that it was ever disabled, so it quietly never gets turned back on. Terraform gives a reviewable diff before any role grant or monitor change ships, and a single source of truth that answers compliance/audit questions ('who can access what, and when did that change') by reading a repo instead of querying ACCOUNT_USAGE and hoping nothing was missed.

Equally important is being explicit about what should stay in Snowsight: personal dev/scratch warehouses, truly ad hoc analysis roles that live for a day, one-off exploratory objects. Forcing every throwaway object through a PR and apply pipeline just recreates the exact friction the team is already complaining about, for things that don't carry security or cost risk. The right scope is standing, shared, and security/cost-relevant objects — production warehouses, resource monitors, functional roles, and grants on shared schemas — while leaving personal and exploratory objects to the UI.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't try to argue Terraform is faster — for a one-off warehouse, clicking genuinely is faster, and pretending otherwise just makes me look out of touch with their actual day-to-day. What I'd actually lead with is: six months from now, can anyone tell me why this role has this grant, or whether that resource monitor someone disabled mid-incident ever got turned back on? That's the real cost of ClickOps — not the two minutes, it's that nothing's reviewable or reconstructable later, and RBAC just drifts.

And I'd be upfront about what I'm not trying to move into Terraform — personal dev warehouses, one-day analysis roles, anything genuinely throwaway. If I tried to force all of that through a PR and apply pipeline, I'd just be recreating the exact friction they're annoyed about, for things that don't actually carry risk. I'd scope it to the stuff that's standing and shared — prod warehouses, resource monitors, functional roles, grants on shared schemas — and leave the scratch stuff to Snowsight.
commonMistakes: Arguing Terraform is faster than the UI for a one-off change, which is usually false and undermines credibility
Making an abstract 'best practice' argument instead of naming a concrete pain point like RBAC drift or a forgotten disabled monitor
Trying to move every object into code, including personal/scratch warehouses, recreating the team's exact complaint
Mandating the change without acknowledging the real short-term friction of adding a deploy step
Not distinguishing security/cost-relevant shared objects from genuinely low-risk personal ones
keyPoints: Doesn't claim Terraform is faster for one-offs; argues from reviewability, auditability, and RBAC drift instead
Names a concrete failure mode (forgotten disabled resource monitor, undocumented stale grants) rather than an abstract best practice
Explicitly scopes what moves to code: standing, shared, security/cost-relevant objects
Explicitly scopes what stays in Snowsight: personal, scratch, one-off exploratory objects
Acknowledges the real short-term friction honestly rather than overselling the change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids the false 'Terraform is just faster' argument
Names concrete pain points (RBAC drift, lost incident changes) over abstract best practice
Explicitly scopes what should move to code vs. stay in Snowsight
Honest about short-term friction instead of overselling adoption

questions.title: Taking Ownership of a Terraform-Managed Platform With Months of Undocumented Manual Drift
questions.prompt: You've just become the owner of a Terraform-managed Azure data platform. The previous owner left, and terraform plan against the current code shows dozens of unexpected changes — resources that were modified directly in the portal during past incidents and never reconciled back into the .tf files. How do you take this over responsibly, and in what order do you act?
questions.modelAnswer:
The first instinct to resist is running terraform apply to 'clean up' the drift immediately — that would blindly revert every manually-made change back to whatever the code says, including emergency fixes that were made during real incidents and may still be the correct state today. The responsible first step is going through the plan output resource by resource and classifying each drifted item as either (a) an intentional fix that should be promoted into the code, meaning the .tf is updated to match what's actually running, or (b) genuine accidental drift that should be reverted to match the declared config. That classification work requires cross-referencing incident tickets/history and talking to whoever on the team remembers the context, not just reading the diff in isolation.

Only after the code has been reconciled to reflect the intentionally-kept changes should any apply run — and that apply should happen in a low-traffic window with a clear rollback plan, ideally validated against a non-prod environment first if one exists. Alongside the reconciliation itself, a strong answer flags the actual process gap: there was no mechanism catching this drift as it accumulated over months, so proposing a recurring drift-detection job (a scheduled terraform plan in CI, alerting on any nonzero diff) is part of taking real ownership, not just the one-time cleanup. The tone throughout should be about fixing the gap, not assigning blame to the person who left for making emergency fixes under pressure.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I would absolutely not do first is just run apply to force everything back to what the code says — some of those manual changes were probably the actual fix for a real incident, and blindly reverting them could reintroduce the exact problem someone fixed under pressure. So step one is going through the plan diff item by item and figuring out, for each one, whether it's a change that should be written back into the code because it's the right state, or something that genuinely drifted and should be reverted. That means digging through incident history and talking to whoever's still around, not just eyeballing the diff.

Once the code actually reflects what should be true, that's when I'd run an apply — and I'd do it in a quiet window with a rollback plan ready, not casually. And I'd use this as the moment to fix the actual gap, which is that nothing caught this drift accumulating for months in the first place — so I'd set up a scheduled plan in CI that alerts the moment there's any drift, so I'm never discovering six months of undocumented changes again. And I'd try not to make this about the previous owner having done something wrong under incident pressure — that's just what happens without a drift-detection process, and now it's mine to fix.
commonMistakes: Running terraform apply immediately to 'clean up' drift without first understanding why each change was made
Treating every drifted resource identically instead of classifying each one as intentional-fix vs. accidental
Blaming the previous owner instead of focusing on reconciliation and the missing process
Reconciling the drift once but not setting up any ongoing drift detection, so the problem recurs
